Introduction Many of us grew up watching the Soviet animated series Kolobki Investigate. The investigation begins with four mysterious holes in a rooftop. The chief detective measures the distance between them with a tape measure and unexpectedly concludes:
— These holes are elephant footprints. His colleague laughs: — Since when do elephants fly? — Then they do. Imagine that I publish a detailed description of a flying elephant. I carefully document its body size, anatomy, diet, behavior, and geographic distribution, include several well-executed scientific illustrations, and the paper is accepted by a peer-reviewed journal.
From that moment on, a publication exists that others can cite.
A scientific paper does more than introduce a new claim. It creates a new object of citation. From that point forward, subsequent authors must acknowledge its existence in the literature, regardless of how convincing the original evidence was. Any future author could truthfully write: “A description of a flying elephant has been published.”
The publication itself does not prove that flying elephants exist. However, it introduces a published report of a flying elephant into the scientific literature. That report may be cited, discussed, compared with new observations, and eventually either supported or refuted—even if the original evidence was weak.
This is precisely why extraordinary claims require an exceptionally strong evidential foundation.
Years later I read Vitaly Tanasiychuk’s book Incredible Zoology. One chapter tells the story of the German zoologist Gerolf Steiner, who described an entirely fictional order of animals so convincingly that many readers initially accepted it as genuine science. There were Latin names, illustrations, morphology, behavior, taxonomy—everything looked like a real scientific publication.
Today these stories make us smile. Yet their value was never the joke itself. They demonstrated how easily scientific form can create an illusion of credibility. They remind us of a simple principle: a story is not evidence, even if it later turns out to be correct.
Scientific mistakes rarely happen because researchers deliberately intend to deceive.
Much more often, the problem begins when a conclusion starts living independently of the observations on which it was originally based.
A photograph does not make a hypothesis true. A video does not replace an experiment. However, without them, an observation gradually becomes nothing more than a retold story. Primary documentation allows the next researcher not merely to trust the author, but to evaluate the original observation independently.
Do not preserve conclusions alone. Preserve the data from which they were drawn.
Without primary data, every discovery eventually turns into a retelling.
This is how an insufficiently documented claim can gradually become a widely cited fact.
If an observation cannot be preserved completely, it should be documented as thoroughly as modern methods allow.
Seeing Once Is Better Than Hearing a Hundred Times An observation exists only once—the moment a researcher makes it. Everything afterwards depends on how completely that observation has been preserved.
The value of photographs, videos, microscope slides, preserved specimens, or living cultures is not limited to illustration. They allow future researchers to examine the original observation rather than relying solely on someone else’s description.
Digital documentation is valuable not only scientifically but educationally as well. It allows biological processes to be shown directly instead of merely described or schematically illustrated.
Why should we preserve video? A photograph captures a moment. A video captures a process. Ваш браузер не поддерживает видео. Development of Sumatra barb eggs. In many cases, the process itself contains information that cannot be extracted from a single image. Time-lapse recordings of embryonic development provide an excellent example.
Time-lapse imaging allows us to observe not only the sequence of changes but also their timing, speed, and the unique characteristics of each developmental stage.
Such recordings make it possible to refine existing descriptions and reveal details that are easily overlooked during occasional observations.
Examples of documented observations:
MicrophotographsGalleryImages, videos, and visual observationsVideo ObservationsMicroscopic ObservationsVideos, time-lapses and microscopic observationsA Brief History of Scientific Documentation Throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, biological illustrations were the primary means of documenting observations. Photography was still limited, so researchers attempted to reproduce what they saw as accurately as possible through scientific drawings. With the development of microphotography and later digital photography and videography, the situation fundamentally changed. Scientists could now preserve not merely their interpretation of an observation, but the observation itself. Modern technologies allow morphology, behavior, and dynamic biological processes to be documented with a level of completeness that was previously impossible. Scientific illustration has not lost its value. It helps emphasize diagnostic features, simplify complex structures, and direct the reader’s attention toward biologically important characteristics. This is precisely why the term scientific illustration exists—it is not a photographic copy of reality, but an interpretation created by the observer.
However, a drawing used as the only evidence of an observation is fundamentally unverifiable.
For this reason, photographs and videos have become an essential part of scientific evidence rather than mere illustrations.
It is impossible to determine whether a drawing reflects an actual observation, the author’s interpretation, or imagination alone. Without primary documentation, a drawing ceases to function as evidence and becomes merely an assertion made by its author.
Modern scientific illustrations should therefore complement photographs and videos—not replace them.
The more extraordinary the conclusion, the greater the requirements for preserving the primary evidence. Why Does This Matter to Aquarists? Many people believe that microscopes are tools only for scientists.
In reality, they are valuable for anyone who wants to make observations rather than simply repeat other people’s conclusions.
A photograph taken through the eyepiece, a video of parasite movement, or a series of images documenting the same specimen are not merely attractive illustrations. They are primary data that can be revisited months or years later, shared with colleagues, and compared with new observations.
Without them, every description gradually becomes a story.
A microscope does more than allow you to see an object. It allows you to preserve an observation.
Questions and Answers I don’t own a microscope. Does this article still apply to me? Yes.
The principle applies to every kind of observation. Whenever it is possible to preserve photographs, videos, or other primary data, it should be done.
Does a photograph prove anything? No.
A photograph records an observation. Scientific conclusions are supported by the combined evidence of independent observations, experiments, and critical analysis.
What if no photograph exists? The observation itself does not lose its value. However, it becomes much more difficult for others to verify independently.
What if the photographs contradict my conclusion? Even better.
The purpose of documentation is not to confirm the researcher’s expectations but to preserve what was actually observed. If primary evidence contradicts a conclusion, then the conclusion—not the evidence—should be reconsidered.
Are scientific drawings no longer useful? They certainly are.
Scientific illustrations emphasize details that may be difficult to recognize in photographs. However, a drawing should never remain the sole evidence of an observation.
Why is this especially important for aquarists? Diseases disappear, fish die, medications are discarded—but photographs, videos, microscope slides, and preserved material remain. They allow us to return later and understand what truly happened.
See also
summary: Why an observation is not yet evidence. Why photographs, videos, and preserved material matter, and how to distinguish a convincing hypothesis from reproducible knowledge.
title: Flying Elephants

content:
What Counts as Evidence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence? Artificial intelligence does not eliminate flying elephants.
It helps them acquire a convincing explanation. Fossa From Storytelling to Documentation This article continues the idea introduced in Flying ElephantsFlying ElephantsWhy science requires more than an elegant hypothesis. The role of photographs, videos, specimens, and primary data in building and verifying ….
At first, knowledge was passed on as a story. Later came more formal descriptions: measurements, characters, Latin names, comparisons, diagnoses. Then biological illustration became a way to show the reader an organism they could not see for themselves.
But a drawing was still not the observation itself. It was the author’s reconstruction of an observation. When a drawing is the only record, it is fundamentally difficult to verify. Years later, we cannot know whether it represents a real observation, the author’s interpretation, or imagination.
Then came photographs and videos. They did not make every conclusion automatically true, but they did make independent verification more realistic. A photograph preserves a moment; a video preserves a process.
Not All Papers Are Documented Equally The problem of weak evidence did not begin with artificial intelligence.
In fish pathology, for example, one often sees the following logic:
a smear or culture was taken -> a bacterium grew -> therefore it caused the diseaseThe Smear Comes First.A reflection on why smear microscopy often matters more than bacterial culture in fish pathology. Real cases, logic, and the danger of ….
But there is a long distance between “a bacterium grew” and “this bacterium caused the death.” We need the clinical picture, photographs of lesions, tissue microscopy, inflammatory response, repeatability, exclusion of background microbiota, spatial association with the lesion, and in some cases experimental confirmation.
If those elements are missing, confidence in the conclusion should decrease. Not because the author is necessarily wrong, but because the reader is not given enough access to the original observation.
The absence of a photograph does not make a conclusion false.
It increases the share of trust placed in the author and reduces the share of independent verification.
When a Drawing Replaces a Photograph For its time, biological illustration was a serious method of documentation. But in a paper where microphotographs, video, slide series, or preserved material are technically possible, a single drawing becomes a weak basis for an unusual conclusion.
In that situation the claim may be extraordinary, while the reader’s ability to verify it remains limited. This does not mean every such paper must be dismissed. But it is an ideal example of the problem: the more unusual the claim, the less it should depend on trust alone.
The more extraordinary the conclusion, the less it should rest on the author’s authority.
When the Photograph Became a Drawing Again For a long time, scientific documentation developed in one direction: from a story toward material that could be shown to another person. A story could be retold. A drawing could be redrawn. But photographs and videos seemed closer to the event itself.
For nearly two centuries, each new documentation technology reduced the need to take the author’s word for it. Drawing gave way to photography; photography gave way to video. It seemed that the evidential foundation was becoming more reliable.
Generative AI has changed that familiar trajectory for the first time. Today it can create not only a story or a drawing, but also a photograph, a video, a voice, a table, a literature review, and a plausible explanation for an event that never happened.
A high-quality photograph or video no longer guarantees that the observation actually occurred. In this sense, we have unexpectedly returned to a situation familiar to researchers of the early twentieth century: the image once again requires trust in its source.
Back to the Future of Evidence 18th century "I saw it" Do you believe me? 19th century "Here is a drawing" Better 20th century "Here is a photograph" Excellent 21st century "Here is a video" Almost ideal AI era "Here is a photograph" Where did it come from? We have not returned to drawings. We have returned to the need to trust the author.
Paradoxically, technological progress has brought us close to the early twentieth century. Back then, a drawing required trust in the observer. Today, photographs and videos increasingly require the same kind of trust. We now sit with images and recordings much as earlier biologists sat with scientific drawings. This does not make AI an enemy of science. It simply makes the origin of data part of the evidence.
The Main Point At first, the weak point was the retelling. Then it was the author’s interpretation. Now the weak point has shifted toward the origin of the data.
Image quality no longer guarantees observation quality.
Image quality increasingly guarantees only image quality.
Text quality no longer guarantees evidence quality.
The quality of an explanation no longer guarantees that the object existed.
Artificial intelligence has not made the scientific method unnecessary. On the contrary, it has reminded us why the method is neededScientific Method. A Practical Guide.How knowledge is formed, why confidence often outpaces understanding, and how the scientific method helps distinguish observation from ….
In the past, it was often enough to ask: “Is there a photograph?” Now we also have to ask: “Where did this photograph come from?”
If video once reduced the distance between observation and reader, the video itself now needs a history of origin. Who recorded it? When? Where? On what object? Is there a sequence of original frames? Are there RAW files? Is there a specimen, a slide, an observation log, a repeated registration, or independent confirmation?
The evidence is no longer the image by itself. The evidence is the traceable path from the object to the image.
Material evidence has not become less important. A microscope slide, fixed material, microbial culture, tissue sample, observation log, series of original images, or preserved object of study remains what it has always been: a way to return to the observation and examine it again.
But in a scientific article, the reader usually does not encounter the object itself. The reader encounters its representation: a photograph, a drawing, a table, a video frame, a description, or the author’s explanation. This is where the new question appears. If an image once helped bring the reader closer to the object, the image itself now needs a traceable origin.
The problem is not that material evidence has disappeared. The problem is that, in the public circulation of knowledge, it is increasingly not the object itself that circulates, but its persuasive digital shell.
Therefore, evidence is no longer the image itself, but the ability to trace the path from the object to the image.
Science spent a long time learning how to preserve observations. Now it also has to learn how to preserve the provenance of observations. FAQ Does this mean photographs and videos are no longer useful? No. They are still essential. But they should be treated as documented data, not as self-sufficient proof. Their value increases when the circumstances of recording, original files, sequence, specimen, or observation log can be checked.
Is this only a problem for AI-generated images? No. AI makes the problem sharper, but the principle is older. Weak documentation, selective images, missing context, and overconfident interpretation existed long before generative AI.
What should be preserved together with an image? As much context as possible: date, place, object, method, equipment, original files, repeated frames, related samples, microscopy slides, records, and any information that allows another person to reconstruct the path from observation to conclusion.
Can a conclusion be correct even if the documentation is weak? Yes. A weakly documented conclusion can still be true. The problem is different: the reader has fewer ways to verify it independently and must rely more heavily on the author’s authority.
What changes for scientific communication? Good communication is no longer just clear writing and strong visuals. It also requires provenance: showing where the data came from and how the conclusion was built from them.
summary: A continuation of ‘Flying Elephants’: a story was never evidence, but now even photographs and videos need a documented origin. What counts as evidence in the age of artificial intelligence?
title: What Is Your Evidence?

content:
Originally, I had no intention of creating a method, a philosophy, or a worldview. I was simply trying to understand questions that seemed incomplete.
Why did the fish die? Why did the treatment fail? Why can the same symptoms lead to different conclusions? Why do many explanations sound convincing while failing to explain the underlying mechanism? Why are some questions considered settled when, upon closer inspection, nobody can confidently explain the details? Over time, it became clear that these problems were not limited to fish pathology. They appear in science, education, engineering, medicine, management, and everyday life. Very often, the disagreement is not about facts but about the way people think. Not about what is known, but about how conclusions are reached.
Gradually, a set of principles emerged—principles that I repeatedly use when working with aquatic organisms, analyzing data, reading scientific literature, and building explanations. That collection of principles eventually became known as the Fossa Method.
In Brief Start with observation, not explanation. Do not confuse description with cause. Every system has constraints. Every model has limits. Simplicity should be the result of understanding. Complexity cannot be eliminated. Demystify knowledge. Look for contradictions. Respect the object of study. The story is more important than the answer. Understanding and knowledge must remain in balance. An explanation should open a door, not close a question. Authority does not replace mechanism. The origin of a claim does not replace its verification. An observed effect does not prove a single cause. I. Observation 1. Start with observation, not explanation The most common mistake is explaining a phenomenon before it has been properly described.
Example.A fish is swimming near the surface and breathing heavily. That is an observation.
The statement “it has a bacterial infection” is already an explanation, and one that has not yet been supported by evidence.
First describe the symptoms. Only then begin looking for their cause.
Start with: “What happened?”, “What did we observe?”, “What did we measure?”, “What was recorded?”
Only afterwards ask: “Why did it happen?”
2. Do not confuse description with cause Description is not explanation.
Example.The statement “the fish died from stress” does not explain the mechanism of death.
What exactly happened?
Did the fish stop feeding? Was there trauma? Failure of osmoregulation? Respiratory impairment? Some other process that can be observed and tested?
The real question is:
“What mechanism produced the observed outcome?”
II. Constraints 3. Every system has constraints A system is a collection of interconnected elements working together toward a particular goal.
In aquaculture, a system may be an aquarium, a filtration system, a population of fish, or even the organization of staff. Changing one element inevitably affects the others.
Example.Increasing stocking density allows more animals to be kept in the same volume of water, but it also increases the load on the filtration system and raises the risk of conflicts between individuals.Constraints cannot be eliminated.
They can only be redistributed.
Every solution creates new constraints.
Therefore, the key question should always be:
“What constraint are we trying to change, and what will appear in its place?”
4. Every model has limits A model is a simplified representation of reality that helps us understand or predict the behavior of a system.
Every model discards some details in exchange for usefulness.
Models can be mathematical, biological, engineering-based, or even verbal.
Example.A medication may work effectively against one parasite while being completely ineffective against another. A method that solves one problem does not automatically become a universal solution.
Likewise, the statement “fin rot is caused by bacteria” is a model that explains some cases of fin damage. However, it does not account for trauma, nutritional deficiencies, hemorrhage, or other factors that can produce similar changes. A model remains useful only as long as we remember its limits.
There are no universal solutions.
There are no medications that solve every problem.
There are no diagnostic signs that apply to every case.
There are no methods that work equally well under all conditions.
The question is not: “Does the model work?”
The more important question is: “Where does the model stop working?”
III. Understanding 5. Simplicity should be the result of understanding Example.The statement “gas bubble disease is caused by excess dissolved gas” simplifies the phenomenon while preserving its mechanism.
The statement “gas bubble disease is caused by bubbles in the water” sounds simpler, but it distorts the process itself.
Simplification is useful.
Oversimplification is dangerous.
A good explanation:
removes unnecessary details; preserves what is essential; reveals the mechanism. A poor explanation:
removes the mechanism itself. 6. Complexity cannot be eliminated Example.Some parasites can be identified using nothing more than a microscope and a simple smear. However, determining the exact nature of certain diseases may require additional investigations. Simplicity is valuable only when it does not distort reality.Some things are genuinely complex.
If the object itself is complex, the description may also need to be complex.
Complexity is not a flaw.
Pretending complexity does not exist is.
7. Demystify knowledge Example.Ziehl–Neelsen staining may appear to be a complicated laboratory procedure. In reality, its purpose can be reduced to two steps: stain the target structure and then remove the stain from surrounding tissues while retaining it within mycobacteria.Complex terminology does not make an idea profound.
Terminology exists for precision, not for authority.
Knowledge should become more accessible, not more mysterious.
IV. Inquiry 8. Look for contradictions Example.If every sign points toward a bacterial disease but bacteriological testing fails to confirm it, that contradiction becomes the reason to reconsider the original hypothesis.The most interesting observations are not confirmations.
The most interesting observations are those that do not fit the existing picture.
They are what move understanding forward.
9. Respect the object of study Example.A poorly performed necropsy can destroy evidence before it is ever examined. Careful work preserves information that may later become essential for understanding the cause of death.A fish is not a statistical unit.
A stain is not a ritual.
A necropsy is not a formality.
Every observation is a source of information.
The goal of the investigator is not to confirm a preferred explanation, but to understand what actually happened.
V. Growth 10. The story is more important than the answer Example.Knowing that physicians eventually began washing their hands before surgery is useful. Understanding which observations led to that conclusion—and why the idea was resisted for so long—is even more valuable.A final conclusion is useful.
But it is often more useful to understand:
how that conclusion was reached; which mistakes were made; which alternatives were considered; why some ideas failed while others survived. The history of discovery is often more valuable than the result itself.
11. Understanding and knowledge must remain in balance Example.It is possible to memorize the life cycle of a parasite without understanding its significance. It is equally possible to speculate about parasites without knowing their biology. Knowledge becomes useful only when facts and understanding support one another.Knowledge without understanding becomes memorization.
Understanding without knowledge becomes imagination.
Growth requires both.
12. An explanation should open a door, not close a question Example.A good explanation allows a person to take the next step independently. It provides a working model without creating the illusion that the subject has been exhausted.A poor explanation says:
“It’s simple. Memorize it and stop thinking.”
The opposite extreme says:
“It’s so complicated that you shouldn’t even try.”
Both positions are equally harmful.
A good explanation sounds more like:
“Here is the simplest model that allows you to begin understanding the phenomenon. It is not the whole picture.”
An explanation should be simple enough to provide an entry point and honest enough to acknowledge that deeper levels of understanding still exist.
13. Authority does not replace mechanism Example.An expert opinion has value, but its value increases when it is possible to understand which observations, data, and reasoning led to that conclusion.A position is not evidence.
Experience alone is not evidence.
A publication record is not evidence.
If a mechanism cannot be explained, authority does not make the explanation correct.
14. The origin of a claim does not replace its verification. Example.The fact that a claim comes from a teacher, a specialist, an organization, or is widely accepted within a professional community does not prove that it is true. The source may increase confidence in the claim, but it does not exempt the claim itself from verification.15. An observed effect does not prove a single cause. Example.The fact that a particular cause can produce an observed sign does not mean that the presence of that sign confirms this cause. Toxic exposure may damage the gills, but damaged gills alone do not prove toxicosis.Questions and Answers Is this a new scientific method? No.
The scientific method existed long before me and works perfectly well on its own.
Fossa Method is not a replacement for the scientific method. It is an attempt to articulate a set of principles that help formulate questions, build explanations, and distinguish observations from interpretations.
Is this a philosophy? Not really.
It is a collection of practical observations that gradually emerged while working with aquatic animals, diagnosing diseases, analyzing data, and studying the history of science.
Why not simply use the scientific method? The scientific method asks:
How do we test hypotheses?
Fossa Method more often asks:
How do we decide which question is worth asking in the first place?
Why is there so much emphasis on constraints? Because many mistakes arise not from a lack of solutions, but from ignoring limitations.
Every solution improves something while creating new problems elsewhere.
Why so much emphasis on observation? Because explanations often arrive before observations.
People see a phenomenon and immediately assign a cause.
There should always be a pause between observation and explanation.
What exactly did we observe?
Why criticize authority? I do not criticize authority.
I criticize situations where authority replaces explanation.
Experience, expertise, and qualifications matter.
But neither position nor reputation constitutes evidence by itself.
Why does a fish-related website contain a page about thinking? Because most articles on this site did not begin with answers.
They began with questions that felt incomplete.
Over time, it became clear that the same principles apply not only to fish pathology, but also to engineering, medicine, programming, education, and scientific research.
What is the core principle of Fossa Method? If I had to choose only one, it would be:
Do not start with an answer. Start with a question.
summary: Not answers, but principles for finding them.
title: Fossa Method

content:
Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. FMC: treatment or ritual? FMC is one of those mixtures that has become so firmly established in aquarium practice that simply using it is sometimes regarded as sufficient action.
The fish is rubbing — FMC.
Mucus appeared — FMC.
Parasites are suspected — FMC.
It is not quite clear what is happening — FMC again.
The problem is not the mixture itself. Formalin, malachite green, and methylene blue do have biological activity and can be useful in certain situations Link: https://fossamethod.ru/ru/posts/medicines_poisons/ . The problem begins when FMC ceases to be a means of acting against particular groups of pathogens and turns into a universal procedure: “give the fish a bath”.
Where did FMC come from in the first place? FMC did not originate as a ten-minute “bath for everything”. Gerald Bassleer’s handbook states that the precursor of the mixture was the Leteux–Meyer Mix, proposed in 1972: 3.3 g of malachite green per 1 L of formalin (Leteux & Meyer, 1972). In 1979, G. Bassleer proposed a stock solution containing three components (Bassleer, 2010):
3.5 g malachite green; 3.5 g methylene blue; 1 L formalin. The recommended dosage is 1 ml per 100 L of water, with a single treatment intended to provide approximately two days of exposure. For ichthyophthiriosis, a water change followed by repeated treatment after two days was recommended (Bassleer, 2010). In other words, the original logic of FMC use was not a few minutes of contact with a concentrated mixture, but prolonged exposure to a comparatively low concentration of the preparation in water.
For comparison, the same handbook gives two fundamentally different treatment regimens for formalin alone (Bassleer, 2010):
1–2 ml per 100 L of water for 12–48 hours; 0.125–0.25 ml per 1 L of water for 30–60 minutes. So even for the same substance, the treatment regimen is determined not only by the name of the drug, but by the combination of concentration and exposure time. This is an important point.
It is not enough simply to say: “Formalin is used against ectoparasites”.
The same formalin can be used as a prolonged treatment at a relatively low concentration or as a short bath at a much higher concentration. These are already different exposure regimens.
This is exactly why the phrase “Let’s bathe the fish in FMC for 10 minutes” tells us almost nothing by itself about whether the treatment is rational.
We need to know:
the concentration of the mixture; the duration of exposure; the suspected pathogen; the sensitivity of the fish; the water conditions; and, most importantly, where this particular regimen came from in the first place. If a source specifies tens of minutes or tens of hours for formalin, but multi-day exposure for FMC, then a ten-minute FMC bath requires its own justification.
The name of a drug does not determine the treatment regimen. The regimen is determined by dose, time, and purpose.
The fact that a fish was bathed does not mean anything was treated The phrase “the fish was bathed in FMC” describes a procedure, but says almost nothing about treatment. To evaluate the result, we need to know at least:
what was suspected what was found before treatment what concentration was used how long the exposure lasted what water the bath was performed in what changed afterward whether the suspected pathogen remained Without this information, FMC easily turns into action for the sake of action. We see that the fish was placed in a colored solution for ten minutes, and psychologically it creates the impression that treatment has been performed. But treatment is defined not by the fact of contact with a drug, but by whether the biological objective was achieved.
“If it got better, then it worked” Not necessarily.
After a bath, a fish may look better for several reasons:
the amount of surface mucus decreased; some ectoparasites actually died or detached; the irritating load on the skin changed; the fish was transferred into cleaner water; for some time, the fish had less contact with the source of reinfection. None of these possibilities by itself proves which component of the mixture had an effect or that the cause of the disease was eliminated. And an improvement in appearance certainly does not always mean that the pathogen has been destroyed.
You can test your reasoning here: https://fossamethod.ru/ru/test/reasoning-test/
Response to treatment is an observation. A diagnosis is already an interpretation of that observation.
They are not the same thing.
What if the parasite really is sensitive to FMC? Then using the mixture may be entirely justified. But even here, questions remain.
At which stage of its life cycle is the parasite sensitive?
Is it on the surface or deeper in the epithelium?
Is the exposure time sufficient?
Could the therapeutic concentration also be too stressful for an already weakened fish? A short bath prescribed simply because “we usually use FMC” looks particularly questionable. If the exposure is insufficient for the treatment target, but sufficient to irritate the gills and skin, we get the worst of both worlds:
the parasite survived the treatment, while the fish received an additional burden.
This is no longer a question of whether FMC is a good drug or a bad one. It is a question of whether the method matches the task.
Why a mixture is convenient — and therefore dangerous A mixture of several active components is psychologically perceived as more reliable:
“If one component does not work, another one will”.
But the same principle works in the opposite direction. Each component has its own toxicity, its own spectrum of activity, and its own limitations. Therefore, adding a second and third substance not only broadens the potential action of the mixture, but also increases the number of factors that must be taken into account.
The more complex the mixture, the less sense it makes to use it without understanding the cause of the disease.
The most inconvenient situation Imagine this: a fish shows nonspecific behavior, for example rubbing against objects. It is bathed in FMC. A day later, the behavior decreases. What has been demonstrated? Practically nothing. We do not know:
whether there was a parasite at all; which parasite it was; whether it was on the skin or gills; whether the mixture affected it; which component of the mixture was significant; whether the behavior disappeared for some other reason. And yet this is exactly how traditions are born:
“FMC helps when the fish is scratching”. After some time, the original observation turns into a treatment rule.
Where are the “traditions instead of science” here? Not in the fact that FMC is an old preparation. And not in the idea that it cannot be used. The problem begins when the name of the mixture replaces the definition of the task. “Do FMC” becomes a goal in itself. Although the correct order is the reverse:
determine what we are observing; formulate a working hypothesis; understand what target we want to act upon; choose the drug and exposure regimen; check the result. If the first three steps are missing, treatment easily turns into a ritual.
A drug does not become scientifically justified simply because it has been used for many years.
But an old drug does not become bad simply because it is old.
There is always one question: why exactly are we using it here and now?
Literature Bassleer, G., 2010. Новый иллюстрированный справочник болезней рыб для декоративных тропических и прудовых рыб: наблюдение, диагностика, профилактика, лечение. Пер. Н. О. Лисова. М.: Учебный центр “Аква Лого”. 232 с. ISBN 978-5-9902638-1-9.
Main source for the FMC formulation cited above, the note that G. Bassleer developed the stock solution in 1979, the dosage of 1 ml/100 L, and the formalin treatment regimens.
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/327941229_New_illustrated_guide_to_fish_diseases
Leteux, F., Meyer, F.P., 1972. Mixtures of malachite green and formalin for controlling Ichthyophthirius and other protozoan parasites of fish. The Progressive Fish-Culturist, 34(1), 21–26.
Classic paper on the malachite green–formalin mixture for treatment of ichthyophthiriosis and other protozoan infections; in later literature, this combination is often referred to as the Leteux–Meyer mixture.
https://doi.org/10.1577/1548-8640(1972)34%5B21:MOMGAF%5D2.0.CO;2
summary: FMC can be useful, but simply bathing the fish proves very little. We examine the origins of the mixture, formalin and FMC regimens, the relationship between dose and exposure time, and how treatment becomes ritual when the drug replaces the clinical question.
title: Traditions Instead of Science. II

content:
Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. “The fish is scratching” A fish rubbing against rocks, substrate, or the bottom is, by itself, an objectively observable behavior. In the literature this behavior is usually described as flashing or rubbing: the fish suddenly contacts a surface with its side, rolls its body along it, and may repeat the movement several times. Such behavior has indeed been described in ectoparasitic infections and other lesions of the skin and gills (Garcia et al., 2014) (Maddocks et al., 2016). At this level, everything is simple: we see an action. The problem begins afterward — when a cause is automatically assigned to that action.
“The fish is scratching.”
Then:
“Probably its gills.”
And then:
“So it must be parasites.”
But how well can we actually determine the cause of such behavior from observation alone?
Imagine a simple experiment The examiner already knows the true cause of the behavior. There are two groups. In the first, the fish have pronounced skin irritation caused by sharply unsuitable pH. In the second, there are large numbers of monogeneans on the gills. In both groups, the fish rub against the substrate and decorations. The pH example is not hypothetical: chemonociceptive receptors responding to low pH and other chemical irritants have been demonstrated in rainbow trout (Mettam et al., 2012). And with monogeneans, flashing is indeed described as a clinical sign (Garcia et al., 2014). The observer is shown only the behavior and asked:
“In which case is the skin irritated, and in which case are the gills irritated?”
And here an uncomfortable question appears:
“How much better would the rate of correct answers be than random guessing?”
If it were significantly better, then there must be specific behavioral features by which one cause can genuinely be distinguished from the other. Those features could then be described, tested, and used. But if we cannot name such features, then the statement:
“It is scratching its gills”
is not an observation, but an interpretation.
What features are we actually using? Can you confidently determine what exactly is causing the rubbing without a scraping, necropsy, or microscopy?
Can you describe:
“how rubbing caused by skin irritation differs from an attempt to scratch the gills?”
Which part of the body touches the surface first? How does the trajectory of the movement change? Is there a characteristic turn of the head? Does the frequency differ? Is the movement linked to respiration? Is there a specific sequence of actions? If such differences exist, they can be studied.
If the answer is reduced to:
“You can just tell by looking at the fish,” then this is no longer a diagnostic criterion…it is the observer’s impression.
And an even more uncomfortable question Are we even sure that a fish can scratch the gills themselves? The gills are located beneath the operculum or inside the branchial cavity and do not directly contact the substrate or a rock. During external rubbing, the fish can mechanically affect the head region, the skin, the operculum, and the margins of the gill opening. But the movement itself does not show that the fish is acting specifically on the gill lamellae. Gill irritation may indeed trigger such a motor response. This is entirely plausible and consistent with descriptions of severe monogenean gill infestations, in which flashing is observed together with respiratory disturbances (Garcia et al., 2014). But the literature usually records the presence of this behavior as a clinical sign rather than describing a specific kinematic pattern that would allow one to say confidently from the movement alone: “the fish is scratching its gills.”
But that is already a different statement:
“Gill irritation can cause flashing.”
It is not the same as:
“The fish is scratching its gills.”
The first describes an association between irritation and behavior. The second assumes a specific purpose of the movement. And that purpose is precisely what we do not know.
Where does observation end? One can say:
“The fish repeatedly makes abrupt lateral contact with the substrate.”
One can say:
“This behavior is often described as flashing and associated with irritation of the skin or gills” (Garcia et al., 2014) (Maddocks et al., 2016).
But the phrases:
“It is itchy.” “It is scratching its gills.” “It is monogeneans.”
— already belong to different levels of interpretation.
And each subsequent level requires additional evidence.
We observe behavior. The cause of that behavior still has to be demonstrated.
References Garcia, R.L., Hansen, A.G., Chan, M.M., Sanders, G.E., 2014. Gyrodactylid Ectoparasites in a Population of Rainbow Trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss). Journal of the American Association for Laboratory Animal Science, 53(1), 92–97.
A clinical case of gyrodactylid infestation in rainbow trout. The authors describe erratic swimming and flashing; they also note that gyrodactylids affect the superficial layers of the skin and gills and can cause irritation, epithelial hyperplasia, mucus hypersecretion, and pruritus, which is inferred from flashing.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3894654/
Mettam, J.J., McCrohan, C.R., Sneddon, L.U., 2012. Characterisation of chemosensory trigeminal receptors in the rainbow trout, Oncorhynchus mykiss: responses to chemical irritants and carbon dioxide. Journal of Experimental Biology, 215(4), 685–693. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.060350
An experimental study of chemically sensitive receptors in rainbow trout. Responses to potentially damaging chemical stimuli, including low pH, acetic acid, and citric acid, were demonstrated. This confirms the physiological possibility of pronounced skin irritation without the involvement of parasites.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22279076/
Maddocks, C.E. et al., 2016. Puffy Skin Disease Is an Emerging Transmissible Condition in Rainbow Trout Oncorhynchus mykiss Walbaum. PLOS ONE, 11(7), e0158151.
In an experiment involving a disease with pronounced skin lesions in trout, flashing was observed: the fish moved down toward the bottom, rubbed their sides against the surface, and rapidly righted themselves. This is a good example of similar behavior arising from skin pathology and not, by itself, indicating a gill localization.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4938586/
summary: Flashing is observable behavior, while “itching,” “gill irritation,” and “parasites” are already explanations. We examine what can actually be observed, which conclusions genuinely follow from the fish’s behavior, and where a familiar phrase turns into an unproven causal model.
title: Traditions Instead of Science. III

Introduction The question “how do you know that?” can be irritating.
Not because it is wrong — but because it is difficult to answer honestly.
In most cases, the answer sounds confident, but is based not on verification, but on habit, experience, or someone else’s conclusions.
The problem is not that we don’t know.
The problem is that we don’t know — and yet we are confident that we do.
How knowledge is formed Knowledge does not appear as a finished answer.
It is assembled gradually — from observations, errors, and attempts to explain what is seen.
The history of science is not a sequence of discoveries, but a chain of refinements.
New data rarely overturn everything at once. More often, they reveal the limitations of previous explanations.
Even simple questions may require years of observation and verification.
Sometimes — a lifetime.
What we often mistake for knowledge what “everyone says” what “has always been done” what resembles a familiar case what conveniently explains what we see All of these can be useful.
None of them, by themselves, constitute evidence.
The most dangerous error is not the absence of knowledge,
but confidence in an explanation that has not been tested.
This becomes especially evident in fish pathology The same symptom may have different causes.
Similar changes may arise from entirely different processes.
The presence of a sign does not imply understanding of the mechanism.
Gas bubbles are not always gas bubble disease.
White spots are not always the same parasite.
Hyperemia is not always inflammation.
Without a method, observation easily turns into speculation —
and speculation into confident explanation.
What the scientific method is in practice The scientific method is not a formula or a set of terms.
It is a way of working with reality.
It includes:
observation recording conditions comparison of signs testing alternative explanations rejecting convenient explanations when they fail under scrutiny It does not guarantee the correct answer.
But it reduces the likelihood of being confidently wrong.
What changes with this approach fewer “instant diagnoses” less ritual treatment better understanding of causes rather than symptoms greater caution in conclusions Most importantly, it allows distinguishing observation from interpretation.
The scientific method does not make the work easier — it makes it more honest.
It does not eliminate errors — but it prevents them from going unnoticed.
It is not a way to always be right — it is a way to avoid being confidently wrong.
Core principles The method does not begin with an answer.
It begins with observation.
1. Data collection Observation must be separated from interpretation.
Record what is actually observed:
fish behavior external appearance changes over time environmental conditions Do not explain — describe.
Not “the fish is sick”, but “the fish is lying on the bottom, respiration is increased”.
2. Recording conditions Every observation has context. Without it, data lose meaning.
Record:
temperature water parameters system changes feeding transfers, stress The same symptom under different conditions represents different situations.
3. Keeping records Memory distorts sequence. Records do not.
Record:
what happened when under what conditions what changed after intervention Without records, it is impossible to distinguish cause from consequence.
4. Comparing signs A single sign does not constitute a diagnosis.
Meaning arises from their combination.
Compare:
which signs match which contradict what is missing despite expectations The absence of a sign can be more important than its presence.
5. Testing alternatives The first explanation is usually the most convenient.
And often wrong.
Ask:
what else could explain this?
If at least one alternative exists, it must be considered.
6. Minimal intervention Intervention changes the system — sometimes faster than we can understand it.
The more simultaneous actions:
the harder it is to identify the cause the higher the risk of incorrect conclusions Fewer actions, but with understanding of their effect.
7. Evaluating outcomes Every action is a hypothesis. The result is its test.
Improvement does not always mean the cause was identified.
Lack of improvement does not always invalidate the hypothesis.
Evaluate:
what changed how quickly how stable the effect is Important The method is not a sequence of steps to complete.
It is a way of thinking applied at every stage.
It does not require complex equipment.
It requires accuracy in observation and honesty in conclusions.
This is what distinguishes knowledge from assumption.
References Ferguson, H.W., 2006. Systemic Pathology of Fish: A Text and Atlas of Comparative Tissue Responses in Diseases of Teleosts, 2nd ed. Scotian Press, London. Kuhn, T.S., 2012. The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, 4th ed. University of Chicago Press, Chicago. Noga, E.J., 2010. Fish Disease: Diagnosis and Treatment, 2nd ed. Wiley-Blackwell, Ames. Popper, K.R., 2002. The Logic of Scientific Discovery. Routledge, London. FAQ Why is one symptom not enough for diagnosis? Because the same sign may result from different processes.
What matters more: experience or method? Method. Experience without verification often leads to errors.
Why avoid immediate treatment? Because intervention alters the system and obscures the cause.
What does “testing alternatives” mean? Considering other possible explanations, not just the first one.
Can mistakes still occur? Yes, but the method reduces confident errors.
summary: A practical view of the scientific method: how to avoid being confidently wrong and distinguish knowledge from assumption.
title: Scientific Method. A Practical Guide.

Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. Knowing the limitations of a method does more than protect us from incorrect conclusions — it tells us where and how to look for what we cannot yet see. Fossa Ziehl–Neelsen staining without the full set of reagents: what can we still learn? If you have a fully equipped laboratory, all the necessary reagents, and suitable working conditions, the answer is straightforward: to test whether bacteria are acid-fast, perform the standard Ziehl–Neelsen stain.
This article is not about replacing the standard method when it is available.
It is about a different situation—one much more familiar to small fish farms, public aquariums, fish pathologists without a dedicated bacteriology laboratory, and even aquarists who own a microscope. There is a diagnostic question, a specimen in front of you, but not the complete set of reagents.
Phenol is toxic, unpleasant to handle, and requires appropriate storage and working conditions.
Strong mineral acids are not exactly things you want to keep next to a microscope “just in case,” either. They have to be obtained, stored, and handled with proper safety precautions.
If part of the classic method is unavailable, does that mean the specimen can no longer tell us anything useful?
You can treat what follows as a little methodological experiment: remove one step, replace another, and see what actually changes. Or you can treat it as a practical necessity.
Either way, the principle is the same:
We need to understand what happens at each step, what that step allows us to learn, and what we can no longer conclude if we remove or change it.
What does the classic method actually do—and where did it come from? Loeffler's methylene blue stain Ziehl–Neelsen stain Mycobacteria are not detected by routine staining.
Ziehl–Neelsen staining is used to detect acid-fast bacteria, particularly mycobacteria (World Health Organization, 1982).
Interestingly, today’s familiar procedure did not appear all at once. What we now call the “Ziehl–Neelsen method” emerged over a remarkably short period through successive changes to existing staining techniques (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017).
In March 1882, Robert Koch, presenting his work on the causative agent of tuberculosis, described staining specimens with a hot alkaline solution of methylene blue, followed by counterstaining with vesuvin (Bismarck brown). The mycobacteria appeared blue against a brown background (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017).
In May of that same year, Paul Ehrlich modified the method. Instead of methylene blue, he used fuchsin or methyl violet in saturated aniline water, then decolorized the specimen with 30% nitric acid and applied a counterstain (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017).
The next step came from Franz Ziehl. In August 1882, he replaced aniline oil with carbolic acid—phenol. The resulting carbol fuchsin was more stable than Ehrlich’s aniline-based solution (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017).
In October 1882, Eduard Rindfleisch proposed heating the specimen directly during staining.
Then, in July 1883, Friedrich Neelsen published his modification of Ziehl’s method: 0.75% fuchsin in 5% carbolic acid, followed by decolorization with 25% sulfuric acid (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017).
So phenol did not enter the procedure as an immutable part of some original recipe.
Ziehl introduced it in place of aniline, Rindfleisch added heating, and Neelsen changed the stain formulation and the decolorization conditions.
Over roughly sixteen months, Koch’s original procedure underwent several substantial modifications before eventually becoming established under the familiar name Ziehl–Neelsen staining (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017).
And the method did not stop evolving there.
In 1887, Gabbett attempted to shorten the procedure by combining acid decolorization with counterstaining. In 1915, Joseph Kinyoun proposed a “cold” method without heating: the fuchsin concentration was increased to approximately 3.1%, phenol to 6.25%, and 3% hydrochloric acid was used as the decolorizer (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017).
Even historically, then, this is how the method developed:
The task remained the same, but the way of accomplishing it changed: reagents were replaced, concentrations adjusted, and exposure conditions modified.
What do we call the classic procedure today? In modern variants, the specimen is stained with heated carbol fuchsin, then decolorized with acid or acid-alcohol and counterstained (World Health Organization, 1982) (World Health Organization, 1999).
One commonly used decolorizer is 3% acid-alcohol:
3 mL of concentrated hydrochloric acid + 97 mL of 95% ethanol.
In this formulation, “3%” refers to the conventional volume ratio of the starting concentrated acid to alcohol, not the exact mass fraction of pure HCl (World Health Organization, 1998).
But this is not Neelsen’s original formula. His 1883 method used 25% sulfuric acid.
The same applies to the primary stain. Neelsen used 0.75% fuchsin in 5% phenol. The composition was subsequently modified many times: Vilchèze and Kremer describe 0.3% fuchsin and 5% phenol for one modern ZN formulation, whereas Kinyoun’s cold method uses substantially higher concentrations (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017).
And this matters for understanding the method:
There is no single concentration forever fixed to the name “Ziehl–Neelsen.” There is a purpose served by each step, and there are conditions under which that step produces a reproducible result.
Knowing a method’s limits means being able to control it If we treat the method as a recipe, it is simple:
fuchsin → heat → acid → counterstain.
But if we ask why each of these steps is performed, things become more interesting:
carbol fuchsin provides intense staining; phenol and heat help the dye penetrate structures that are otherwise difficult to stain; acid decolorization tests whether stained structures can retain fuchsin; counterstaining makes the background easier to examine microscopically. That is why omitting one step does not necessarily make the entire result worthless.
Some observations remain possible, even though certain conclusions can no longer be drawn.
Know the limits of a method, and you can work with it.
Ignore those limits, and all you can do is follow the recipe.
If bacteria are not visible, we do not know whether they are absent from the tissue or simply cannot be detected by the method we used.
If staining makes them visible, that is already an observation. We can assess their shape, abundance, distribution, and relationship to pathological lesions.
But what this observation actually demonstrates depends on how the image was obtained. We can see red rods; whether they would retain fuchsin after acid treatment is another question.
What if there is no phenol? Phenol is part of classic carbol fuchsin for a reason, not merely “because that is how it has always been done.” Traditionally, it is considered to facilitate dye penetration through the lipid-rich mycobacterial cell envelope. Heating also promotes staining.
But does that really mean fuchsin cannot enter the bacterium without phenol?
This question had already been tested experimentally, long before my own experiments—and, particularly interestingly, with pathogens of fish as well.
In 2000, Vinnie Della Speranza and Rena Fail published a paper with the rather expressive title “Phenol Myth Unveiled! Were Ziehl-Neelsen and Kinyoun Mistaken?”
The authors initially tried replacing phenol with surfactants. Then they decided to see what would happen if the surfactants were removed as well, leaving only an aqueous solution of basic fuchsin.
The result was unexpected: a 0.5% aqueous fuchsin solution heated to 60 °C produced good staining of mycobacteria in 15 minutes. At room temperature, the same solution remained ineffective even after an hour of exposure. The paper includes photomicrographs of Mycobacterium avium and M. tuberculosis stained without phenol (Della Speranza & Fail, 2000).
So removing phenol does not, in itself, prevent staining. The conditions under which the dye is applied still matter.
In 2008, Carol McCollough tested this approach specifically with pathogens of fish and aquatic invertebrates.
She used 0.5% aqueous fuchsin at 60 °C for 15 minutes, followed by acid-alcohol decolorization. The preparations revealed M. marinum in the kidney of a goldfish and M. chesapeaki in the spleen of a striped bass.
The study was not limited to mycobacteria. Positive staining was also obtained for several microsporidians, haplosporidians, and myxosporeans. Not every organism stained equally well: for example, fixed spores of Kudoa clupeidae did not retain fuchsin after decolorization (McCollough, 2008).
In other words, phenol-free staining had already been used in fish pathology to detect mycobacteria in fish tissues, including the spleen.
In 2020, Gomes and colleagues carried out another comparative study, introducing a modification called GASMoC.
Unlike the earlier experiments, they used 1% aqueous fuchsin at just 37 °C for 15 minutes. Specimens were stained in parallel: some with classic carbol fuchsin, others without phenol. Both groups then underwent the same acid-alcohol decolorization step.
Of 12 specimens with previously confirmed tuberculosis, GASMoC detected acid-fast bacteria in all 12, while the conventional Ziehl–Neelsen method detected them in 11. All seven negative controls remained negative with both methods.
The researchers found no statistically significant difference between the results. Moreover, bacilli stained using GASMoC were often more intensely colored and easier to distinguish against the surrounding tissue.
The paper provides direct comparative photomicrographs of the phenol-containing and phenol-free methods. The authors also successfully tested the method on zebrafish tissue containing Mycobacterium marinum (Gomes et al., 2020).
Thus, phenol was not essential for detecting acid-fast bacteria in the specimens examined. Changing the composition of the primary stain did not eliminate the diagnostically relevant result.
There is an important detail here: all three studies retained the acid decolorization step. The authors removed phenol but continued to test whether fuchsin was retained after acid treatment.
So this is not merely about seeing red rods without phenol. It is about detecting acid-fast structures using a modified primary stain.
Of course, this does not mean that any protocol can be changed arbitrarily while always producing the same result. But it does show that the same diagnostic characteristic can be detected under different staining conditions.
If phenol helps a dye enter a bacterium, that does not mean entry is impossible without phenol. The question is not whether the reagent is inherently indispensable, but whether the required result can be achieved without it.
If phenol is unavailable, we need not frame the question as:
“How can we pretend that we are still performing Ziehl–Neelsen staining?”
Instead, we can ask:
Can we achieve sufficient staining of the structures we want to examine by another means?
In my own preparations, intense heating with fuchsin without phenol made red, rod-shaped bacteria clearly visible. This does not prove that phenol and heat are fully interchangeable, nor does it turn the procedure into classic Ziehl–Neelsen staining. But something important did happen for the practical task:
Bacteria that had previously been difficult to distinguish became visible.
We can assess their morphology, abundance, and location within the tissue. That is useful information in its own right.
What if there is no acid? Here the boundary is even clearer. It is the acid decolorization step that establishes the characteristic for which the method is called “acid-fast”: after stringent differentiation, some structures lose their fuchsin, while others retain it. Therefore, if no acid decolorization was performed, we cannot claim:
“Acid-fast bacteria were detected.”
Acid-fastness simply was not tested. But that does not make everything done before this step meaningless. If intensive staining makes numerous rod-shaped bacteria clearly visible in a tissue specimen, we now know they are present. We can observe their shape, the density of their clusters, their distribution, and their relationship to pathologically altered areas.
We simply do not yet know one particular property—whether they would retain fuchsin after acid differentiation. And those are fundamentally different things.
— Loading image… Annotations: Off After intensive staining with fuchsin, the preparation can be counterstained. In my case, I used Loeffler’s counterstaining method. The rods that had initially taken up the stain intensely remained bright red.
This contrast makes rod-shaped bacteria easy to see. But by itself, it is not a test of acid-fastness.
And this opens up another possibility that is easy to overlook if we regard acid as a mandatory part of any fuchsin stain. Without acid decolorization, we do not see only structures capable of withstanding acid. Other bacteria, spores, parasitic oocysts, and various tissue structures may also remain stained. Sometimes that is a disadvantage: the background becomes more intensely colored, making the specimen harder to interpret. But at other times, this broader picture is precisely what we need.
By omitting acid decolorization, we lose selectivity for acid-fastness, but we may reveal structures that the acid step would have made invisible.
This is not an invented approach. For example, modified acid-fast fuchsin stains are used to detect the oocysts of Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, and Cystoisospora. These are parasites, not fungi. In standard variants, acid decolorization is generally not omitted, but its conditions are modified; oocyst staining may be uneven, and some oocysts may remain completely unstained (CDC, n.d.) (CDC, n.d.).
Another example is bacterial endospores. Dorner’s method uses heated carbol fuchsin, and one modification works without a separate acid decolorization step. This is no longer a stain intended to detect mycobacteria: it uses a familiar dye to reveal a different target (American Society for Microbiology, 2016).
So the question is not always how to make a stain “correct” for detecting one particular pathogen. Sometimes it is more useful to reveal a wider range of structures first, assess their shape and location, and then decide which findings need specific confirmation.
One organ — three staining variants For this comparison, I used material from the same spleen of an angelfish, which had numerous pale lesions.
Here is a gross photograph of the spleen.
From this material, I prepared specimens using three staining procedures:
Without phenol and without acid decolorization.
Without phenol, but with decolorization using 5% sulfuric acid.
With phenol, followed by acid decolorization.
The same microscope and camera were used in every case.
With phenol and acid Without phenol, with acid Without phenol or acid
The result was interesting: rod-shaped bacteria of similar morphology were clearly visible in all three preparations. Moreover, the rods retained their staining after treatment with 5% sulfuric acid even when phenol had been omitted.
In separate earlier experiments, I also observed rods retaining their stain after 30 minutes of exposure to 10% sulfuric acid.
Of course, three preparations from one organ do not constitute a full comparative study of method sensitivity. But they allow us to see directly that omitting phenol does not necessarily prevent staining the bacteria of interest.
And here is the central question: if we can obtain the result we need after changing the reagent composition, what is truly essential to the method, and what is merely one way of achieving the goal?
This does not mean that phenol is useless or that all three variants are equivalent. It means that the result can be examined, compared, and evaluated, rather than merely checked against a recipe.
Here is another example. In a different preparation, we replace fuchsin with an aqueous solution of malachite green, followed by acid decolorization and counterstaining with phloxine.
Malachite green with heating, 5% sulfuric acid for 2 minutes, followed by phloxine counterstaining. Carbol fuchsin followed by acid decolorization.
Can you see the morphological similarities?
Malachite green, acid decolorization, and phloxine counterstaining. Both preparations show elongated rod-shaped structures, some forming characteristic clusters. The color, contrast, and staining characteristics differ, but the similarities in shape and arrangement are clearly visible.
We replaced not only phenol but also the primary dye itself. Yet the morphological features we are interested in remain clearly observable.
Of course, similarities between the images do not prove that the different preparations contain the same microorganisms. However, they demonstrate that useful morphological information can be obtained using different staining approaches.
And now a question: does every diagnostic task really require the Ziehl–Neelsen method?
Sometimes the goal is not to confirm a particular property of a bacterium, but first to detect suspicious structures, examine their morphology, and decide what to investigate next.
Can you find mycobacteria without color?
Select the squares where you think the mycobacteria are located. Then reveal the color version. Reveal colors Reset Does it have to be that particular acid? Even the history of the classic method shows that the important thing is not the “magic” of one specific acid, but how it decolorizes the specimen and whether the structures of interest retain their staining.
Different acid-fast staining protocols use different reagents and concentrations for differentiation: for example, sulfuric acid at various concentrations or acid-alcohol containing HCl (World Health Organization, 1982; World Health Organization, 1999). WHO materials also mention the use of hydrochloric, sulfuric, and nitric acids (World Health Organization, n.d.).
The purpose of acid treatment is to distinguish structures that lose their staining readily from those that retain fuchsin under specified conditions. But changing the acid, its concentration, or the duration of treatment does not automatically produce the same diagnostic test.
This leads to a perfectly reasonable experimental question:
What happens if we use a concentrated citric acid solution instead of the usual decolorizer? Which structures lose their staining, and which retain it?
If the background becomes decolorized while some rods remain red, that is an interesting experimental observation. But this observation alone does not establish acid-fastness according to the standard criterion.
Important: this is an experimental substitution of a reagent, not a validated Ziehl–Neelsen variant. The standard manuals considered here do not list citric acid as a routine decolorizer; comparability of the results must be established using control preparations.
So concentration is not some sacred number written in a recipe. The type of acid and the duration of exposure matter as well. With milder treatment, fuchsin may remain in the surrounding tissues; if the goal is simply to see the rods, this is not always a problem. With more aggressive decolorization, even the bacteria of interest may lose their staining. We need to understand what the rods actually withstand, rather than treating every trace of retained red staining as proof of the same property.
The goal is not to discover the one “correct” acid concentration in every situation. The goal is to understand what happens when the stringency of decolorization changes.
Even acid-fastness is not a constant property We are accustomed to describing mycobacteria as “acid-fast bacteria,” as though this were an unchanging property of every cell at every moment of its existence.
But that is not entirely true.
Vilchèze and Kremer discuss the so-called “Koch paradox”: when Mycobacterium tuberculosis enters a persistent, nonreplicating state, some bacteria can become ZN-negative—no longer detectable by standard acid-fast staining (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017). This state is often called dormant, or “sleeping,” although the bacterium is not literally asleep.
This has been linked to changes in lipid metabolism and cell-envelope structure. The exact mechanism behind the loss of acid-fast staining, however, remains incompletely understood: changes in the envelope may impede dye penetration or reduce the cell’s ability to retain the dye after decolorization.
Here, knowing about the Koch paradox suggests a simple practical step. Imagine a familiar situation: the spleen or kidneys contain numerous granulomas, the appearance suggests mycobacteriosis, but no rods are detected with Ziehl–Neelsen staining. What next? We can stain the material again with fuchsin, but this time without acid decolorization.
Perhaps the irregular, unevenly stained rods with familiar morphology—previously undetectable after acid treatment—will become visible. We have not proved that they are mycobacteria, but we have obtained another observation and a new direction for investigation.
This is not an attempt to “fix a negative Ziehl–Neelsen result” at any cost. We are simply using another staining possibility: first examine the morphology without acid-based selection, then compare the finding with the tissue changes. Omitting acid broadens the range of structures that remain visible, so similar bacterial morphology alone does not establish a diagnosis.
Vilchèze and Kremer’s work concerns primarily M. tuberculosis. It is an important reason not to treat a negative ZN result as proof that mycobacteria are absent, but it is not a reason to automatically attribute every ZN-negative granuloma in a fish to dormant mycobacteria.
In other words, properly performed Ziehl–Neelsen staining does not answer the broad question “Are there any mycobacteria here?” It answers the narrower question: “Are there structures here that exhibit acid-fast staining under these conditions?”
The practical implication is important.
If rod-shaped bacteria retain staining after standard acid differentiation, we are observing acid-fastness—but we still have not identified their genus or species.
If no bacteria are detected with ZN staining, that does not yet prove that the specimen contains no mycobacteria.
During persistent infection, part of the bacterial population may remain invisible to standard acid-fast staining, leading to an underestimation of the bacterial burden (Vilchèze & Kremer, 2017).
Staining does not tell us a bacterium’s name. It shows us how the bacterium behaves under a particular treatment.
This is where the importance of understanding a method’s limits becomes especially clear.
We see rods — we know that rod-shaped bacteria are present in the tissue.
We perform standard acid decolorization and the rods retain their staining — we observe acid-fastness, but still do not know their species.
We obtain a negative Ziehl–Neelsen result — we still do not know whether mycobacteria are absent from the tissue.
What do we actually know in the end? Imagine a specimen in which numerous thin red rods become clearly visible after heating with fuchsin.
If their morphology allows us to confidently distinguish rod-shaped bacteria, we can describe their presence in the material examined. But not everything stained by fuchsin is necessarily a bacterium: other structures may be present in the preparation.
We can assess:
their shape and size; their spatial arrangement; their abundance and the density of clusters; the tissue context; their association with granulomatous or other pathological changes; whether the finding is repeated in different areas of the specimen. Morphology alone, of course, cannot establish the bacterial genus, let alone the species.
But a lack of complete identification does not make the observation useless.
Seeing bacteria and identifying their species are two different diagnostic tasks.
Similarly:
Seeing stained bacteria and demonstrating their acid-fastness are also two different tasks.
If a higher level of certainty is required, we can perform a complete acid-fast staining procedure, culture, PCR, or another confirmatory test.
But if those options are unavailable at the moment, that is no reason to pretend the microscope showed us nothing at all.
So where does “tradition instead of science” come in? The standard method is not the problem.
A standard method is valuable precisely because its conditions are defined, tested, and reproducible.
The problem begins when we stop asking why each step is performed and merely repeat the familiar sequence like a ritual:
“You cannot see anything without phenol.”
“It has to be this particular acid because that is what the instructions say.”
“If one step is missing, the entire result is automatically worthless.”
A scientific approach asks a different question:
What exactly changed in the result when we changed the method?
If we do not understand what a stain actually demonstrates, we may never even think to examine the specimen in another way. If you fail to recognize the limits of your knowledge, you also fail to notice the questions you have yet to ask.
Remove acid decolorization, and you lose the right to claim acid-fastness, but you have not necessarily lost the diagnostic information.
You may even see structures that would have remained invisible after acid treatment.
Change the staining conditions, and you can assess whether you have obtained the image you needed.
Substitute another acid, and you can test which structures become decolorized and what the result allows you to claim.
Sometimes changing a method narrows the range of justified conclusions while expanding the range of things we can observe. The boundary is not between a “correct” and an “incorrect” ritual, but between what we have actually tested and what we merely assume.
You can change a method. But when you do, the limits of what you can legitimately conclude change with it.
How should the result be described? If the classic procedure was not followed in full, we cannot hide behind its name.
Appropriate wording:
“A modified heated fuchsin stain without acid decolorization was used. Intensely stained rod-shaped bacteria were detected in the tissue material. Their acid-fastness was not assessed.” Inappropriate wording:
“Ziehl–Neelsen staining was performed; acid-fast bacteria were detected.”
Those are two different claims.
Conclusion Knowing a method’s limits means being able to control it.
If a method has been modified, there is no need either to pass it off as the standard procedure or to automatically dismiss the information it provides. Sometimes, by leaving out one step, we lose diagnostic selectivity but gain the opportunity to notice something we could not see before.
What we need to do is much simpler:
State precisely what we did, what we observed, and what actually follows from it.
