content:
Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. “Granulomas Found—So It Must Be Mycobacteriosis” During fish necropsies, whitish nodules in the spleen, liver, or kidneys often raise suspicion of mycobacteriosis. This suspicion is reasonable: granulomatous lesions are indeed characteristic of many cases of mycobacterial infection. The mistake comes at the next step—when a morphological finding is treated as an already established etiology.
Three concepts need to be kept separate: a visible nodule, a granuloma, and mycobacteriosis. They are related, but they are not equivalent.
What Are We Actually Seeing? Two photographs of fish spleens show numerous whitish lesions. Their gross appearances are similar, but microscopy reveals different findings.
Fish spleen with numerous whitish lesions. Mycobacteria were detected by microscopy. Fish spleen with numerous whitish nodules. Other intracellular microorganisms were found in the microscopic preparation. The color and distribution of visible lesions do not reveal their cellular architecture. Therefore, a white nodule seen at necropsy should not automatically be called a granuloma. The tissue must first be examined—for example, by histology.
What Is a Granuloma Made Of, and Why Does It Form? In its classical definition, a granuloma is an organized collection of mature mononuclear phagocytes, primarily macrophages. These cells engulf and process microorganisms, foreign particles, and debris from damaged tissues. Other cells may be present in a granuloma, and its center may contain necrosis, but neither feature is required by the definition (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2018).
If a macrophage can eliminate an irritant, a prolonged organized reaction may not develop. But when material persists, is difficult to break down, or is too large, additional cells are recruited and a localized lesion forms.
Importantly, the persistent material does not necessarily come from outside the body. The reaction may also develop around remnants of the organism’s own damaged tissues. Thus, the equation “granuloma = infection” is incorrect even at the level of mechanism.
Granulomas can develop in response to various bacterial, fungal, and parasitic infections, as well as certain noninfectious processes. A granulomatous response describes the host’s reaction; its etiology must be established separately.
Why Shape and Necrosis Do Not Provide a Diagnosis When examining granulomatous lesions, we assess their organization, size, number, the presence of necrosis, the prominence of peripheral cellular layers, and the development of a connective-tissue capsule.
The full article presents a useful diagram with a single compact center, a large irregular center, and adjacent lesions that may merge. This is a model of possible patterns of organization, not a way to identify a pathogen reliably from a lesion’s outline.
Schematic illustration of factors that may influence the appearance of granulomatous lesions. Necrosis—the death of cells within a lesion—does occur in mycobacteriosis, but it is not unique to it. Conversely, the absence of necrosis does not rule out mycobacterial infection. The same applies to capsule thickness and the regularity of lesion contours.
Within a group of fish, similar lesions may develop a similar structure. This can help compare cases and suggest a shared pathological process, but it does not make any particular granuloma shape unique to a specific pathogen.
Not Every Round Structure Is a Granuloma The full article shows structures in neon tetra kidneys that are tentatively interpreted as mineral concretions; some are surrounded by features resembling a granulomatous response. Fibrous nodular structures in gudgeon kidneys are also shown. These findings are deliberately described with caution: without further confirmation, not every nodule or granuloma-like cellular arrangement should be assigned to a specific pathological process.
View these specimens in the interactive microscope in the F.O.S. article.
Many Granulomas—Does That Mean a High Bacterial Load? Not necessarily. The number and integrity of granulomas depend not only on the pathogen, but also on how the immune response is organized. Well-formed lesions may help contain infection. When this organization breaks down, mycobacteria may multiply extensively while the granulomas deteriorate.
Moreover, experimental models of Mycobacterium marinum infection in zebrafish have shown that, under certain conditions, mycobacteria can exploit the recruitment and movement of macrophages to spread further (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2015).
A granuloma, then, is not always a static capsule surrounding a pathogen, nor is it a “counter” of bacterial cells.
From a Finding to an Etiological Diagnosis It helps to distinguish different levels of evidence.
Gross examination. Whitish nodules or lesions are visible in particular organs. This describes their external appearance, not their cellular composition. Tissue microscopy. We assess whether granulomatous architecture is confirmed, what occupies the center of a lesion, and whether necrosis or other changes are present. Special staining. Ziehl–Neelsen staining can reveal structures that retain the dye after acid decolorization. Finding such structures, especially within lesions, strengthens the suspicion of mycobacteriosis. However, acid-fastness does not identify a bacterial species, and a negative stain alone does not rule out infection. Pathogen identification. When necessary, culture, PCR, sequencing, or a combination of methods may be used, taking sample quality and the clinical context into account. For more on what this staining method actually tests, see “Tradition Instead of Science I. Method”.
This sequence does not imply that every test is available in every case. Its purpose is to make clear the level of certainty reached by our conclusion.
Where Is the Boundary? “Multiple whitish lesions were found in the organs” is a gross observation.
“Granulomas were confirmed in the tissue” is a morphological conclusion.
“Acid-fast rod-shaped bacteria were detected” is the result of a special investigation.
“Mycobacteriosis was diagnosed” is an etiological diagnosis that requires consideration of the evidence as a whole.
We should move from one statement to the next as evidence becomes available—not merely because these findings often occur together.
A granuloma helps characterize a pathological process. Its appearance alone, however, cannot establish the cause.
References Pagán, A. J., Ramakrishnan, L. (2018). The Formation and Function of Granulomas. Annual Review of Immunology, 36, 639–665. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-immunol-032712-100022 Pagán, A. J., Ramakrishnan, L. (2015). Immunity and Immunopathology in the Tuberculous Granuloma. Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Medicine, 5, a018499. https://doi.org/10.1101/cshperspect.a018499 Other versions: F. — the story of two spleens, without technical terminology · F.O.S. — the full analysis, examples, and interactive microscopy collections.
summary: A visible nodule is not necessarily a granuloma, and a granuloma does not necessarily mean mycobacteriosis. We explain the mechanism, morphological features, and steps involved in verifying a diagnosis.
title: Granulomas in Fish: What Their Structure Reveals—and What It Cannot Prove

Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. If We Change the Staining Method, What Remains of the Result? In diagnostics, it is tempting to see a protocol as a fixed sequence of mandatory steps. If one reagent is missing, the method cannot be performed—and the specimen supposedly has nothing more to tell us.
But this confuses two different questions: Can we perform the standard test? and Can we still obtain useful observations from the specimen? The answers are not always the same.
Ziehl–Neelsen staining, used to detect acid-fast bacteria, including mycobacteria, is a good example. Conventional versions use carbol fuchsin, heating, acid or acid-alcohol decolorization, and a counterstain. Each step has its own function.
If we change a step, we need to understand what information we have preserved and what we have lost.
What Happens During Staining? Loeffler's methylene blue stain Ziehl–Neelsen stain Mycobacteria are not detected by routine staining.
Fuchsin stains structures in a specimen. In the conventional method, phenol and heat help the dye penetrate structures, including bacteria that are difficult to stain by ordinary methods.
Then comes a fundamentally different step: acid treatment. It removes the dye from some structures, while others continue to retain it under the specified conditions. This is how we demonstrate acid-fastness—the ability to retain a stain after a particular decolorization procedure.
A counterstain helps distinguish tissues and the background.
So omitting phenol and omitting acid are not equivalent changes. In the first case, we alter the conditions of primary staining. In the second, we remove the actual test for acid-fastness.
Heating: 40 °C, 60 °C, or All the Way to Boiling? In the conventional Ziehl–Neelsen method, carbol fuchsin is heated after it has been applied to the specimen, usually until vapors begin to appear. Some protocols associate this visual cue with approximately 60 °C. The dye is kept heated for several minutes (often 3–5 minutes), without allowing it to boil or dry out (ASM protocol; comparative study).
But the appearance of vapors is not the same as boiling: liquids evaporate at temperatures below their boiling points. Thus, “until vapors appear” is only an approximate guide, not a precise way to control temperature. For a reproducible modified procedure, it is better to record the measured dye temperature, exposure time, and concentration.
Why not heat it further? Boiling is not the goal of the method. It increases evaporation and can cause the dye to dry out or splatter. With phenol, chemical safety is an additional concern. It is also important to distinguish heat fixation of the specimen before staining from heating the dye during staining—these are separate operations.
Phenol-free methods use different conditions. Some studies used 0.5% aqueous fuchsin at 60 °C for 15 minutes; the GASMoC method used 1% aqueous fuchsin at 37 °C for 15 minutes. Staining at 37–40 °C is therefore possible in principle, but 40 °C is not a universally validated temperature: any protocol has to be evaluated in terms of dye concentration, exposure time, and specimen type. These findings apply to specific studies; they do not establish that all the conditions are interchangeable.
Can We Do Without Phenol? Yes, under certain conditions. This is supported by published research, not just isolated observations.
Della Speranza and Fail (2000) showed that a 0.5% aqueous solution of basic fuchsin, without phenol, could stain mycobacteria at 60 °C in 15 minutes. At room temperature, the same approach performed considerably worse under their conditions. So the outcome depends not only on the composition of the stain, but also on how it is applied (2000 study).
McCollough (2008) used staining with 0.5% aqueous fuchsin at 60 °C for 15 minutes to examine pathogens of aquatic animals, including Mycobacterium marinum in the kidney of a goldfish (study).
Gomes et al. (2020) compared conventional staining with a modified phenol-free procedure using 1% aqueous fuchsin at 37 °C for 15 minutes, both on clinical samples and on zebrafish tissue containing M. marinum. In the samples studied, the new procedure was not inferior to the conventional method for detecting acid-fast bacteria. However, the sample size was small, and the findings cannot simply be generalized to all specimens and conditions (GASMoC study).
One point matters in all these cases: acid decolorization was retained. The researchers changed the primary stain, but they did not abandon the test for the property they were investigating.
Therefore, the absence of phenol does not, by itself, make it impossible to detect acid-fast bacteria. But the conditions of a particular staining procedure must be evaluated, and its results need appropriate controls.
What Happens If We Leave Out the Acid? Suppose that, after intensive fuchsin staining, red rod-shaped bacteria are visible in the tissue. We can examine their shape, approximate numbers, distribution, and association with altered regions of the organ.
But if acid decolorization was not performed, acid-fastness was not tested. We cannot report “acid-fast bacteria detected,” however convincing the rods may look.
There is another side to this change. Acid can remove stain not only from the background but also from structures we might want to examine. Without acid, the microscopic field may look more cluttered, but additional objects may remain visible. This can be useful during exploratory examination, although it reduces the selectivity of the procedure.
Therefore, staining without acid decolorization is not a simplified Ziehl–Neelsen test. It is a different procedure with a different set of permissible conclusions.
One Organ, Three Methods For my own comparison, I used specimens prepared from the same angelfish spleen, which contained numerous pale lesions. The specimens were stained in three ways:
With phenol, followed by acid decolorization. Without phenol, but with decolorization using 5% sulfuric acid. Without phenol and without acid decolorization. All specimens were imaged using the same microscope and camera.
Rod-shaped bacteria stained with phenol and acid decolorization. Rod-shaped bacteria stained without phenol, with acid decolorization. Rod-shaped bacteria stained without phenol or acid decolorization. Similar red rod-shaped bacteria were observed in all three preparations. This is consistent with the possibility of staining without phenol, including retention of the stain after acid treatment.
However, specimens from a single organ do not allow us to calculate sensitivity or specificity or demonstrate that the three procedures are equivalent. This is a comparison of observed results, not validation of a new diagnostic method.
What If We Use a Different Acid? Different acids and decolorization conditions have been used in historical and modern acid-fast staining methods. Thus, no single acid is a universal, indispensable component of every variant of the method (Vilchèze and Kremer, 2017).
But this does not mean that any acidic solution provides the same test. The type and concentration of the acid, as well as the duration of treatment, affect which structures lose their stain.
For example, a concentrated citric acid solution could be considered an experimental decolorizing agent. Even if the background loses its color while the rods remain red, this is not automatically equivalent to a standard test. Appropriate positive and negative control specimens would be needed for comparison.
A Negative Staining Result Has Limits, Too There is another reason not to turn a staining result into a definitive diagnosis.
Even mycobacteria do not always exhibit acid-fastness to the same degree. In Mycobacterium tuberculosis, states have been described in which some cells are poorly detected or not detected at all by conventional staining. This is discussed in the work on the so-called “Koch’s paradox” (Vilchèze and Kremer, 2017).
For fish diagnostics, the cautious principle is this: a negative staining result does not, by itself, prove that mycobacteria are absent. But neither can every negative stain of fish tissue be explained by “dormant” mycobacteria. That is only one possible explanation and would require investigation.
Conversely, a positive acid-fast staining result does not automatically establish the genus or species of the bacteria. Additional testing, such as PCR or culture, may be needed for identification.
How to Describe the Finding Correctly If heated fuchsin was used without subsequent acid decolorization, the report should describe both the procedure and what was actually observed:
A modified fuchsin staining procedure with heating, but without acid decolorization, was used. Intensely stained rod-shaped bacteria were observed in the tissue. Their acid-fastness was not assessed.
It would be incorrect to state that standard Ziehl–Neelsen staining had been performed and that the presence of acid-fast bacteria had been demonstrated.
The key distinction: omitting a step does not invalidate the observations already made, but it changes the limits of the conclusions we can draw. A method is not a magic formula that must be recited word for word; it is a sequence of actions, each of which should answer a specific question.
For the history of these modifications, the exact experimental conditions, and a detailed bibliography, see the full F.O.S. version. The F. version tells the same story with almost none of the laboratory details.
summary: The roles of phenol, heat, and acid, illustrated by three staining approaches applied to specimens from an angelfish spleen.
title: Phenol-Free Staining: What Changes in the Method and the Conclusions

content:
Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. When Red Rods Matter More Than the Name of the Method Loeffler's methylene blue stain Ziehl–Neelsen stain Mycobacteria are not detected by routine staining.
Imagine examining tissue from a sick fish under a microscope. You can see cells, patches of material, and fragments of tissue. But are there any bacteria among them? It’s hard to tell.
Laboratories use special staining methods for situations like this. A stain makes structures visible that would be difficult to distinguish in an unstained specimen.
In this case, we use fuchsin—a dye that stains certain cells and bacteria bright red. It lets us see structures under the microscope that would otherwise be difficult to make out. In the conventional method, phenol is added to the fuchsin. Phenol is a chemical that does not stain anything by itself, but helps the dye penetrate bacterial structures that are difficult to stain. This mixture is called carbol fuchsin. Heating also matters. In conventional Ziehl–Neelsen staining, the dye is gently heated until faint vapors appear—approximately 60 °C. It does not need to boil. Heat helps fuchsin stain bacteria, but that does not mean hotter is always better.
After staining, the specimen is treated with acid. The acid removes the dye from many structures, while certain bacteria remain red. This is how we test for acid-fastness—the ability to retain the stain after acid treatment.
But the necessary reagents are not always available. So what should we do—put the specimen aside and accept that we cannot learn anything from it?
I’d rather ask a different question: what can we see if we change the usual staining procedure? And, just as importantly, what can we legitimately conclude from the result?
One Angelfish, Three Specimens Let’s take the spleen of an angelfish with numerous pale spots. We prepare specimens from this tissue and stain them in three different ways.
In the first, we follow the conventional procedure: a stain containing phenol, followed by acid treatment. In the second, we leave out the phenol but keep the acid treatment. In the third, we use neither phenol nor acid decolorization.
Why do this? Not to give an old method a new name. We want to see how much each step actually matters.
The results are easy to see. All three preparations contain clearly visible small red rods, similar in shape and distribution. We use the same microscope and camera for comparison.
Red rod-shaped bacteria: staining with phenol and acid decolorization. Red rod-shaped bacteria: staining without phenol, but with acid decolorization. Red rod-shaped bacteria: staining without phenol or acid decolorization. This is not a large scientific study, just a comparison of several specimens from the same organ. These images are not enough to claim that all three methods are equally reliable. But they do demonstrate one useful point: changing the procedure does not necessarily make the result disappear.
Why You Cannot Simply Skip the Acid There is an important distinction here.
Some bacteria remain red even after acid treatment. This property is called acid-fastness. It is what the well-known Ziehl–Neelsen staining method is designed to test.
If we did not treat the specimen with acid, we did not perform that test. Even if the rods look exactly like those in another preparation, their color alone does not justify calling them acid-fast.
But does that make the rods we can see useless? Not at all. We can still examine their shape, number, distribution, and the areas of tissue in which they appear.
The distinction is simple:
Seeing bacteria is one task. Testing whether they are acid-fast is another. Identifying which bacteria they are is a third.
One photograph cannot answer all three questions at once.
So What Is the Phenol For? Phenol is part of the conventional staining solution and helps the staining process. But “helps” does not mean “cannot be done without it.”
Researchers have already shown that, under certain conditions, bacteria can be stained with fuchsin without phenol. Temperature turned out to be particularly important. For example, aqueous fuchsin was successfully used at 60 °C for 15 minutes, including on fish tissues (McCollough, 2008). Another study achieved staining at just 37 °C for the same 15 minutes by changing the dye concentration (Gomes et al., 2020). Both methods retained the subsequent acid decolorization step.
So the question “40 degrees, 60 degrees, or all the way to boiling?” cannot be answered with a single number. The result also depends on the solution’s composition and the staining time. 37 °C was tested in a particular protocol; that does not prove every staining procedure will work at 40 °C. And boiling is not necessary at all.
The point, then, is not whether phenol is good or bad. The question is what function it serves, and whether that function can be achieved another way.
Why This Matters When working in diagnostics, you may lack not only reagents but also time, equipment, or the opportunity to send a sample to a laboratory right away.
In that situation, it is easy to fall into one of two extremes. The first: “If I cannot do it exactly by the book, there is no point looking at anything.” The second: “I see red rods, so the diagnosis is confirmed.”
Both get in the way of thinking.
A microscope can provide useful information even when a definitive answer is still out of reach. We just have to avoid claiming more than the evidence shows.
You can change a method. But then you need to ask yourself again: “What did I actually test? What did I observe? And what do I still not know?”
That is the difference between following instructions and understanding why those instructions exist.

summary: Can a specimen still provide useful information when some reagents are unavailable? A story of one experiment and three staining methods.
title: Red Rods: Why I Changed the Usual Method

content:
Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. Two Spleens. One Diagnosis? Here are two photographs of fish spleens. Both have numerous whitish spots and nodules. At first glance, they look similar.
Someone familiar with fish diseases might suspect mycobacteriosis. Or, out of habit, use an even simpler term: fish tuberculosis.
There is a reason for that suspicion. Mycobacterial infections often cause nodular lesions in fish organs. But similar appearances do not necessarily mean the same cause.
Let’s see what was found in these two cases.
Fish spleen with numerous whitish lesions. Mycobacteria were detected by microscopy. Fish spleen with numerous whitish nodules. Other intracellular microorganisms were detected in the microscopic preparation. And there is the surprise: they look alike from the outside, but the microscopic findings are different. Seeing only the white spots, we could not have known in advance what we would find inside.
So What Is a Granuloma? Sometimes, a necropsy reveals pale nodules. When the tissue is examined under a microscope, some of these turn out to be organized clusters of immune cells. These are called granulomas.
One job of these cells is to engulf and remove things that are causing trouble. They can take up bacteria, the remains of dead cells, and other material. But not everything can be broken down and cleared away quickly.
When the problem persists, immune cells may gather around it and form an organized focus. This is one way a granuloma can develop.
An important distinction: not every white nodule seen at necropsy is necessarily a granuloma. To call something a granuloma, we need to examine its structure, not just its color and outward shape.
Why a Granuloma Does Not Identify a Single Culprit Imagine finding such a cluster of cells in a tissue. What does it tell us?
Perhaps the body is trying to contain bacteria. But the cause might also be another microorganism, a parasite, a foreign particle, or material left behind by damaged tissue that the body cannot easily remove.
In other words, a granuloma shows how the body is responding to a problem, but it does not tell us what that problem is.
Think of it as finding a repair crew at work. The workers tell us that something has happened, but without inspecting the site, we cannot know whether the problem is a broken pipe, faulty wiring, or a damaged wall.
Granulomas have another twist: in certain infections, a cluster of immune cells may not only contain the pathogen but also help it spread. That is why the number and appearance of granulomas cannot be used as a simple count of the bacteria present.
What If We Find Red Rods? One way to investigate suspected mycobacteriosis is to stain a tissue preparation. After treatment with a dye and an acid, some bacteria remain red. This property is called acid-fastness.
If rod-shaped bacteria with these staining properties are found in the affected tissue, the suspicion of mycobacteriosis becomes stronger. But their color alone does not tell us which bacterial species they belong to. Further tests may be needed.
Conversely, if acid-fast bacteria are not detected, that does not mean every possible cause of the lesions has been ruled out.
We explain the staining procedure and its limitations in “Tradition Instead of Science I: Method”.
So What Should We Write in the Report? Start with what has actually been established.
If all we can see at necropsy are whitish nodules, we can describe them exactly that way. If microscopy confirms that they are granulomas, we can write: “multiple granulomas.”
But a diagnosis of mycobacteriosis requires evidence of its own.
Similar shape, white color, necrosis, or a large number of nodules cannot replace an investigation into their cause.
A granuloma is not a diagnosis. It is a trace of the body’s response. The task of diagnosis is to find out what made that response necessary.
Want to explore the topic further? F.O. — how granulomas form and what morphology can tell us · F.O.S. — a full analysis with microscopic preparations and references.
summary: Two similar-looking spleens, two different microscopic findings. A story about why white nodules and granulomas are not diagnoses in themselves.
title: White Spots in Fish Organs: Is It Tuberculosis?

content:
Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. “Granulomas? Then it must be fish tuberculosis” When granulomas are found in the parenchymal organs of a fish, the next thought often comes almost automatically:
Mycobacteriosis.
Or, more simply:
Fish tuberculosis.
The association is understandable. Granulomas are indeed very common in fish with mycobacteriosis. The problem begins when a characteristic response of the organism is treated as the name of the causative agent. First, we need to establish what we actually saw.
What is a granuloma? Typical granulomas associated with mycobacteriosis. One classical definition of a granuloma is a compact, organized collection of mature mononuclear phagocytes, primarily macrophages (large immune cells that engulf bacteria, viruses, and cellular debris).
Necrosis (irreversible cell death), giant cells (very large, usually multinucleated cells), lymphocytes (a type of immune cell), and other familiar components of granulomas may be present, but none is essential to the definition. What matters is the organized accumulation of mature macrophages (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2018). A simpler way to express the modern definition is:
A granuloma is an organized attempt by macrophages to deal with something that a single macrophage could not handle.
Pagán and Ramakrishnan offer a particularly clear model:
If the first phagocyte engulfs an object and manages to destroy it, there is no need for a granuloma.
If the object persists, is difficult to break down, or is too large, additional cells are recruited and a more organized structure forms (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2018).
In other words, the very appearance of a granuloma tells us primarily that:
something was persistent enough that an ordinary phagocytic response (an immune defense in which cells called phagocytes, such as macrophages, recognize, engulf, and digest foreign particles, bacteria, and dead cells) was insufficient.
It does not even have to be “foreign” As early as 1925, Margaret Reed Lewis observed the behavior of monocytes in culture. These cells responded not only to tuberculosis bacteria or experimentally introduced coal particles.
They also engulfed:
the body’s own melanin granules (small intracellular compartments, or organelles, that contain the natural dark pigment melanin); dead granulocytes (a type of white blood cell containing prominent granules with biologically active substances involved in immune defense and inflammation); erythrocytes (red blood cells that transport oxygen from the respiratory organs to the tissues and carry carbon dioxide back). During cultivation, monocytes developed into macrophages (large immune cells that engulf bacteria, viruses, and cellular debris). After several days, cells that had engulfed difficult-to-remove material acquired an epithelioid appearance, and some fused to form multinucleated giant cells (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2018).
Thus, the distinction between “self” and “foreign” is not the only thing that matters in the development of a granulomatous response.
Another question is more important:
Can the material be removed quickly, or not?
A dead cell does not literally become a “foreign body.” It remains material belonging to the organism. But when a cell breaks down, it leaves behind membranes (thin, flexible layers of lipids and proteins that enclosed the cell and its internal organelles, separating them from the surroundings), lipids (a broad group of fats and fat-like organic substances that are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents), proteins (complex organic molecules made of amino-acid chains that serve as structural components and carry out many biological functions), and other cellular debris (the remains of destroyed cells and tissues after cell death, inflammation, or injury). This material has to be cleared away. If it persists in the tissues, phagocytes (including macrophages, monocytes, and neutrophils) continue to respond, attempting to engulf and remove the remnants of destroyed cells. Such a response can become prolonged and contribute to chronic granulomatous inflammation.
That is why the equation:
“granuloma = infectious agent”
is too simplistic from the outset.
A mechanism older than fish The granulomatous response appears to be much older than one might expect of the complex cellular immune system of vertebrates. Granulomas are formed not only by mammals, birds, and fish. They have also been described in mollusks, worms, and insects (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2018). One example is particularly striking. A parasitoid wasp lays an egg in a fruit-fly larva. The egg is too large for an individual phagocyte to engulf. Instead, cells surround it and form an organized granuloma-like structure. The underlying task remains the same:
If you cannot destroy it, isolate it.
In the freshwater clam Corbicula fluminea, a granulomatous response can even develop around the animal’s own larvae when, for some reason, they are not released normally. Their remnants are subsequently resorbed (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2018). It is hard to imagine a clearer example of why the presence of a granuloma alone tells us nothing specific about mycobacteria.
Many different causes A granulomatous response may be triggered by very different agents. In their review, Pagán and Ramakrishnan list bacteria, fungi, protozoa, helminths, and viruses among the infectious causes. Granulomas may also arise around foreign material and in a variety of noninfectious inflammatory conditions (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2018).
So this line of reasoning:
granuloma → mycobacterium
does not work.
A better formulation is:
granuloma → a persistent factor → determine what that factor is.
In aquarium practice, mycobacteriosis is indeed among the first possibilities to investigate when multiple granulomas are present. But the leading differential diagnosis is not yet an established diagnosis.
Mycobacteria The story becomes even more interesting with mycobacteria. For a long time, a granuloma was imagined almost as a fortress built by the organism around a bacterium:
Here are the bacteria; here is a wall of immune cells around them; the infection has been contained.
This mechanism does exist. But it turned out to be only part of the picture. Studies of Mycobacterium marinum in zebrafish have shown that pathogenic mycobacteria can exploit the very process of granuloma formation:
An infected macrophage attracts new macrophages. It dies. Another macrophage engulfs its remains, together with the bacteria inside. Now the next macrophage is infected. It, too, becomes part of the granuloma. In these experiments, the number of infected macrophages began to rise sharply after cellular aggregates formed. At the same time, the number of viable mycobacteria increased (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2015).
The result is almost paradoxical:
the organism recruits cells to contain the infection, while the bacterium uses the arriving cells as new sites for replication.
Nor is a mature granuloma necessarily a sealed capsule. Cells continue to enter and leave it, and infected macrophages can move away from the primary focus and contribute to the formation of new lesions (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2015).
That makes the modern view of granulomas far more interesting than the old one:
A granuloma can both contain an infection and help the pathogen spread.
Which process predominates depends on the stage of infection, the state of the immune response, and the properties of the pathogen itself.
Many granulomas — many bacteria? Not necessarily.
A granuloma reflects more than the number of pathogens present. It reflects how the organism interacts with them. When the cellular response is effectively organized, well-defined granulomas may develop. When macrophage function is impaired, lesions may become disorganized and necrotic even while the bacterial burden is very high. In experimental models where tumor necrosis factor (TNF)—a signaling protein through which immune cells regulate inflammation and defense against infection—was disrupted, mycobacteria proliferated actively while granulomas lost their organized structure (Pagán & Ramakrishnan, 2015).
Thus, “generalized mycobacteriosis, but very few well-formed granulomas” is not a contradiction at all. Sometimes it may indicate the opposite of what one would expect: the immune system is failing to contain the infection effectively.
What if we use Ziehl–Neelsen staining? This is where we move from a suspicion to the next level of evidence.
If numerous rod-shaped bacteria are found within granulomas and retain carbol fuchsin after acid decolorization, the hypothesis of mycobacteriosis becomes considerably stronger. But here, too, we must avoid skipping another step. Ziehl–Neelsen staining demonstrates acid-fastness. It does not automatically establish the species of bacterium.
More on this: Traditions Instead of Science I. Method: Staining and the Limits of Interpretation
Species-level identification requires other methods, such as culture, PCR, sequencing, or a combination of these approaches.
A granuloma tells us:
An organized chronic tissue response is taking place.
Staining tells us:
Structures with particular staining properties are present here.
Molecular or culture-based methods bring us closer to answering:
Who exactly is present?
One does not replace the other.
Sometimes a granuloma has nothing to do with bacteria Here are two fish spleens with numerous whitish lesions. In the first case, mycobacteria were detected by microscopy. In the second, intracellular microorganisms morphologically resembling Histoplasma were found.
The first photograph is included specifically for comparison. The two organs show similar changes to the naked eye, but microscopy reveals very different findings. This is precisely why numerous whitish nodules do not, by themselves, identify the cause.
Fish spleen. Multiple small whitish granulomatous lesions. Mycobacteria were detected by microscopy. Fish spleen. Multiple whitish nodules of varying sizes. Microscopy revealed intracellular microorganisms morphologically resembling Histoplasma.
It is possible to find numerous granulomatous lesions without detecting acid-fast bacteria in them. The cause may be an entirely different process—for example, a parasitic infection. That is why it is better to describe what is actually visible first:
“multiple granulomas”
and only then investigate their etiology.
Because the entry:
“multiple granulomas — mycobacteriosis”
quietly turns an observation into a diagnosis.
Granuloma shape matters too Liver of Apteronotus albifrons with granulomatous lesions (acid-fast bacteria detected):
— Loading image… Annotations: Off Concretions in the kidney of a neon tetra. Microscopic preparation of a neon tetra kidney. Round and oval structures of different sizes, with well-defined margins and heterogeneous contents, tentatively interpreted as mineral concretions. Some are surrounded by cellular structures resembling a granulomatous reaction. No mycobacteria were detected, and similar structures were not found in other organs.
— Loading image… Annotations: Off A granuloma is not merely a “nodule” in tissue. Its organization also matters. The morphology of a lesion often depends on what lies at its center, and how many such centers there are. We can distinguish several patterns schematically.
Factors influencing granuloma shape A single compact center If the initiating factor is small, the response may organize around one center and produce a relatively round, compact granuloma. A large or irregularly shaped center If the underlying structure is large, uneven, or difficult to remove—such as a parasitic structure, a concretion, or a substantial area of tissue breakdown—the resulting granuloma may follow its contours and become less regular in shape. Two adjacent centers Sometimes two lesions lie close together in the tissue. Their outer zones of response may merge, creating the impression of a single complex granuloma. But two distinct centers suggest two closely spaced granulomas rather than one irregular lesion. Necrotizing and non-necrotizing granulomas Fibrous nodular lesions in the kidneys of a gudgeon (Gobio gobio). The lesions range from 0.5 to 8 mm in size. Their central regions have a homogeneous appearance. No acid-fast bacteria were detected.
— Loading image… Annotations: Off Another important feature is whether necrosis is present at the center.
When cells in the center of a granuloma break down and form an amorphous mass, the lesion is termed a necrotizing granuloma.
Central necrosis is characteristic of many mycobacterial granulomas, but it also occurs in other diseases. Conversely, mycobacteriosis can occur without necrosis.
In some fungal and parasitic diseases, numerous well-organized granulomas without central necrosis may be present even in severe disseminated disease.
Within a single epizootic episode, granulomas often have similar structures. When the same agent affects a relatively uniform group of fish, the granulomatous response—its shape, capsule development, and the presence or absence of necrosis—may recur in a fairly consistent pattern. Yet this morphotype (a set of characteristic structural and shape-related features) reflects the interaction between a particular pathogen and a particular host; it is not a universal property of the pathogen.
What surrounds a granuloma? It is important to examine not only the center of a granuloma but also its periphery. In some cases, the boundary with the surrounding tissue is poorly defined. In others, the lesion is surrounded by several layers of macrophages, other inflammatory cells, and connective-tissue elements.
Over time, a dense connective-tissue capsule may form around a granuloma. Its thickness and prominence depend on the duration of the process, the nature of the irritant, and the tissue response of the host.
Where does “tradition instead of science” come into this? Not in the association between granulomas and mycobacteriosis itself. That association is real and can be very useful in practice. The problem arises when a probable cause is treated as the only possible cause simply because we are accustomed to seeing the two together.
The shortcut “saw a granuloma → wrote ‘tuberculosis’” saves time.
But it discards the most interesting part of diagnosis. What initiated the granuloma? Are bacteria present within it? Are they acid-fast? Is an infectious agent present at all? What is happening in the surrounding tissue? Is the process localized or generalized? Only after asking these questions do we have grounds to move from a morphological feature toward a diagnosis.
A granuloma is not a diagnosis.
It is a trace of the organism’s response.
And the task of diagnosis is to find out why that response was needed.
References Pagán, A.J., Ramakrishnan, L., 2018. The Formation and Function of Granulomas. Annual Review of Immunology 36, 639–665.

A review of granuloma formation and function, including the definition of a granuloma, its evolutionary origins, infectious and noninfectious causes, responses to foreign material and persistent endogenous structures, and both the protective and pathological roles of granulomatous inflammation.
Pagán, A.J., Ramakrishnan, L., 2015. Immunity and Immunopathology in the Tuberculous Granuloma. Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Medicine 5, a018499.
https://doi.org/10.1101/cshperspect.a018499
A review of the interaction between mycobacteria and granulomas. Models including Mycobacterium marinum infection in zebrafish demonstrate that granulomas do not merely contain infection: mycobacteria can exploit macrophage recruitment and death to multiply and spread.
summary: Granulomas do not necessarily mean mycobacteriosis. Shape, size, necrosis, and capsule development characterize a pathological process but do not identify its cause. Using examples of different lesions in fish, we examine the limits of morphological diagnosis and the danger of turning observations into ready-made diagnoses.
title: Traditions Instead of Science IV. Diagnosis.

content:
Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. FMC In aquarium fish care, FMC sometimes becomes the answer before the question has even been formulated. A fish rubs against decorations, mucus production increases, a parasitic infection is suspected—and a treatment bath is prescribed.
This does not necessarily mean the decision is wrong. FMC does contain biologically active substances. The problem arises when the name of the mixture replaces the rationale for using it, and performing a bath is taken as proof that treatment was effective.
To distinguish between these situations, we need to understand what FMC contains, where its treatment regimens came from, and which parameters determine the outcome.
What Is FMC? In the formulation discussed here, FMC combines three components:
Formalin — an aqueous solution of formaldehyde, used against certain external pathogens of fish. Malachite green — a dye with antiparasitic activity. Methylene blue — another dye with its own biological activity. The mixture may act on several biological targets. However, its components have toxic effects as well as useful biological activity. The argument that “three substances are present, so at least one is bound to work” does not stand up to scrutiny.
Even when the composition is known, the name FMC alone cannot tell us which regimen will be both safe and effective. We also need to know the concentration, duration of exposure, condition of the fish, characteristics of the suspected pathogen, and water conditions.
Where Did the Treatment Regimen Come From? The full F.O.S. article examines the history of the mixture through its sources. An early precursor was a combination of malachite green and formalin described by Leteux and Meyer in 1972 for controlling Ichthyophthirius and other protozoan parasites of fish (publication).
According to Gerald Bassleer (2010), he proposed a three-component FMC formulation in 1979. The stock solution described contained 3.5 g each of malachite green and methylene blue per litre of formalin. The regimen given was 1 mL of stock solution per 100 L of water, with exposure lasting approximately two days; for ichthyophthiriasis, another treatment was to follow a water change.
This is a historical account of a specific formulation and regimen, not a universal instruction for treating any fish. Its relevance here is different: it involved prolonged contact with a relatively dilute mixture, not an arbitrarily chosen ten-minute bath.
For comparison, the same reference separately described two regimens for formalin alone: 1–2 mL per 100 L for 12–48 hours, and 0.125–0.25 mL per litre for 30–60 minutes.
We must not conflate formulations when comparing them: formalin regimens cannot automatically be treated as FMC regimens. Even with a single active substance, changing both the concentration and the duration produces a different exposure regimen.
Why Exposure Time Cannot Be Separated from Concentration Exposure time is the period during which the fish remains in contact with the preparation. Concentration tells us how much of the active substance is present in the water. Together, they define the exposure conditions, but they do not in themselves guarantee effectiveness.
A statement such as “ten minutes in FMC” tells us too little to assess the outcome unless we know:
the exact formulation and actual concentration of the solution; the duration of contact and water conditions; which organism or pathological process the treatment is intended to eliminate; how susceptible that target is to the chosen exposure; whether the individual fish can tolerate the procedure; what was observed before and after treatment. The parasite’s life-cycle stage also matters. If the susceptible stage is inaccessible to the substance during a short bath, the presence of an active preparation does not mean the target has been reached. Whether the parasite is on the body surface or within tissues also affects its likelihood of coming into contact with the substance.
Therefore, this argument does not work: “Formalin acts against ectoparasites; FMC contains formalin; therefore, ten minutes in FMC is enough.” The essential link is missing: evidence for that particular regimen against the suspected target.
A preparation is defined not only by its composition but also by the conditions under which it is used. Treatment is justified when the regimen matches the specific objective.
What Does Improvement After a Bath Mean? Imagine a fish that rubs intensely against objects and produces large amounts of mucus before treatment. The day after a bath, the irritation appears reduced and the fish looks better.
That is an observation. But several explanations are possible:
some external parasites may have died or become detached; the amount of mucus on the body surface may have decreased; water conditions may have changed when the fish was transferred; contact with a possible source of infection may have been reduced; the fish’s behaviour may have changed for reasons unrelated to the preparation. Without an initial diagnostic assessment and a follow-up examination, we cannot determine which explanation applies. Even if the parasite burden has genuinely decreased, this does not prove that the pathogen has been completely eliminated or that the effect will persist.
A common reasoning error occurs here: “the fish improved after treatment” becomes “the treatment eliminated the cause of the disease.” Evidence is needed to bridge these two statements.
What Should Be Checked Before and After? Before evaluating a treatment bath, it is useful to formulate a working hypothesis—for example, that the fish has an external parasitic infestation. Where feasible, microscopic examination of suitable material can be performed on the living fish, documenting the suspected pathogen, the severity of the lesions, and the fish’s clinical condition.
The next step is to define not merely a preparation but an objective: to reduce or eliminate a particular parasite burden at an acceptable level of risk to the animal. After treatment, we check whether that objective was achieved, rather than looking only for an improvement in appearance.
If there was no initial examination, conclusions about efficacy will be limited. If the suspected pathogen was not assessed before and after treatment, we cannot confidently say it has disappeared.
The same applies when a fish rubs against objects. Rubbing is not, by itself, a specific sign of parasitic disease and does not automatically determine either the diagnosis or the treatment regimen.
Why a Multicomponent Mixture Requires Extra Care Several active substances can tempt us into thinking: “If one does not work, another will.”
But the other side of that reasoning is additional limitations and a potential toxic burden. If the chosen exposure time is too short to affect the parasite but long enough to irritate the fish’s skin or gills, the procedure may worsen the fish’s condition without solving the original problem.
This is not an argument against FMC itself. The mixture may be justified when the target, suitable regimen, and criteria for evaluating the outcome are known. The problem is prescribing it without those conditions.
Where Does Treatment End and Ritual Begin? A reasoned approach to treatment follows a sequence:
Observation → working hypothesis → biological target → choice of preparation and regimen → evaluation of the outcome.
If we start at step four and then treat any improvement as confirmation of the diagnosis, we end up in a circular argument. The fish was rubbing against objects → FMC was administered → the fish rubs less → therefore, “FMC treats rubbing.” Yet the original cause remains unknown.
A treatment bath is a procedure that has been performed. Treatment efficacy is a conclusion that requires evidence.
The age of the preparation is beside the point. An old remedy does not become wrong simply because it is old, but neither does long-standing practice prove that an arbitrarily chosen regimen is effective.
References Bassleer, G. (2010). Новый иллюстрированный справочник болезней рыб для декоративных тропических и прудовых рыб [New Illustrated Guide to Fish Diseases for Ornamental Tropical and Pond Fish]. Moscow: Aqua Logo. 232 pp. ISBN 978-5-9902638-1-9. Cited for the historical FMC formulation and treatment regimens; bibliographic details and discussion appear in the full article. title: FMC: Why a Treatment Bath Is Not the Same as Effective Treatment

content:
Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. Ten Minutes — and the Fish Is Cured? Imagine a familiar situation in an aquarium. A fish rubs against rocks, there is more mucus on its skin, and it behaves restlessly. What is happening? Perhaps parasites are irritating it. Or perhaps the cause is something entirely different.
But the decision has already been made: “Let’s give it an FMC bath.”
The fish is placed in water containing the treatment for ten minutes and then returned to its aquarium. The procedure is complete. It may seem that all we have to do now is wait for the fish to recover.
But what actually happened during those ten minutes? Did the treatment have enough time to affect the parasites? And were parasites even the cause of the problem?
What Is FMC? FMC is the name of a mixture used to treat certain diseases in fish. The formulation discussed here contains:
Formalin — an aqueous solution of formaldehyde that acts against some external pathogens but can also harm the fish itself. Malachite green — a chemical dye with antiparasitic activity. Methylene blue — another dye with biological activity. Each component has its own properties and limitations. Combining them does not create a universal cure for every disease.
And there is an important distinction: “This product works against some parasites” and “Any bath with this product will help” are not the same claim.
Why Ten Minutes Is Not a Magic Number Treatment depends not only on what we add to the water. Just as important are the concentration of the treatment in the water and how long the fish is exposed to it.
Consider two different approaches. In one, a small amount of the product is added to a large volume of water and left to act for a long time. In the other, a more concentrated solution is used for a short period. These are different exposures, even if the product name on the label is the same.
When the FMC mixture was originally proposed, the approach involved prolonged exposure to a low concentration — for roughly two days. Formalin on its own has also been used in other regimens, including short baths. But that does not mean the exposure time used for formalin alone can automatically be applied to FMC. The details and references are available in the F.O. analysis.
So where did those ten minutes come from? If the only answer is “That’s how we’ve always done it,” then we have a habit, not an explanation.
What If the Fish Looks Better After the Bath? Suppose that by the next day the fish has almost stopped rubbing against rocks. There is less mucus on its skin. Does that mean the FMC worked?
Possibly. But not necessarily.
Some parasites may have died or detached. Some of the mucus may have washed away. The fish may have been moved into more suitable water. The irritation may have decreased for an entirely different reason. An improvement in appearance alone cannot tell us exactly what happened.
The opposite situation is also possible: the fish looks better, but the pathogen remains. The problem then returns, even though the bath initially seemed successful.
To tell these possibilities apart, we should at least try to establish what was present before treatment and what changed afterward. For example, we might examine material from the skin or gills under a microscope, when feasible and justified.
An improvement in appearance is an observation. Elimination of the cause of disease is a conclusion that requires additional evidence.
What If Parasites Were Not the Reason the Fish Was Rubbing? Fish can rub against objects for different reasons. That behavior alone tells us neither the name of the disease nor which medicine to use.
If we have not identified the cause, then after the bath we cannot confidently say what we were actually treating.
A particularly troubling possibility is that the parasite is resistant to the chosen treatment or protected within the tissues, while the product further irritates the skin and gills of an already weakened fish.
In other words, we tried to fight the disease but placed an additional burden on the animal without solving the original problem.
So What Counts as Treatment? A medicated bath is an action. Treatment is an attempt to achieve a particular biological outcome.
First, we need to understand what is happening to the fish. Then we need to decide which cause we intend to address. Only then can we choose an appropriate method and check whether the thing we were trying to change has actually changed.
Sometimes FMC will be a justified choice. Sometimes a completely different intervention will be needed. And sometimes the first step should not be adding a chemical at all, but checking the conditions in the aquarium and investigating the problem.
We gave the fish a bath — that’s a fact. Whether we cured it remains to be demonstrated.
That is why turning treatment into a familiar ritual is dangerous. Not because FMC is “bad” or “outdated,” but because no medicine can replace the question: “What exactly am I treating this fish for?”
Want to explore the subject in more depth? F.O. — why concentration and exposure time matter more than a familiar product name · F.O.S. — a full analysis of FMC, its history, and the literature.
summary: A fish rubs against objects, so it gets an FMC bath. But what did we actually do, and how can we tell whether it helped?
title: We Gave the Fish a Bath. But Did We Cure It?

Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. “The fish is scratching”: where observation turns into diagnosis A fish suddenly brushes the side of its body against the substrate, sometimes repeating the movement several times. In the literature, this behavior is described as flashing or rubbing. It has been reported in some ectoparasitic infestations, skin diseases, and gill disorders.
The movement itself is observable. Yet a familiar explanation often comes before any investigation:
“The fish is scratching” → “It is scratching its gills” → “So it must have gill parasites.”
The first step is an everyday description of behavior. The second is an assumption about the site of irritation. The third is an assumption about its cause. “Every new step requires data that motion alone cannot provide.”
The question is not whether flashing can accompany a parasitic infestation. It can. The question is: how specific is this behavior, and can its characteristics distinguish between possible causes?
Why the same behavior need not have the same cause The original F.O.S. article proposes a thought experiment.
Imagine two groups of fish:
the first has pronounced irritation of the external surfaces, for example due to a markedly unsuitable pH; the second has confirmed monogeneans on the gills. Suppose both groups rub against the substrate. An observer sees only recordings of their movements, does not know the examination results, and must decide which condition is present in each group.
If a specialist is confident that they can distinguish the two, we can ask a testable question: which specific features of the movements are they using? The point of first contact? Head position? Turning angle? Speed? Repetition rate? Association with respiratory movements?
Those features would then need to be defined in advance and tested against independent video recordings for which diagnoses have been established by other methods. Ideally, the person evaluating the recordings would not know which group each fish belongs to. Only then could we discuss the diagnostic accuracy of the feature, rather than the observer’s personal confidence.
Important: this is a proposed way to test a hypothesis, not a published experiment demonstrating identical movement patterns under different conditions. The sources cited below do not establish a test capable of reliably distinguishing gill lesions from skin irritation on the basis of a single movement.
What research actually supports Parasites and flashing Garcia et al. (2014) described erratic movements and flashing, among other signs, in rainbow trout affected by gyrodactylid parasites. This shows that rubbing can occur during a parasitic infestation. But observing a sign in infected fish does not mean that it occurs only with that infestation or that it identifies the affected body region without further examination.
Garcia et al., 2014
Skin disease and flashing Maddocks et al. (2016) described similar movements in rainbow trout with puffy skin disease, a condition associated with pronounced skin changes. The fish descended to the bottom, rubbed their sides against it, and rapidly righted themselves.
This is an important counterexample to the claim that “this movement necessarily means the fish is scratching its gills”: similar behavior has also been described in fish with skin disease.
Maddocks et al., 2016
Can water cause irritation without parasites? Mettam et al. (2012) investigated sensory nerve endings in the head region of rainbow trout. They recorded responses to a range of chemical irritants, including acidic solutions and low pH.
This provides a physiological basis for considering environmental irritants independently of parasitic infestation. However, the study measured receptor activity, not differences between types of flashing. It cannot be cited as direct experimental evidence that fish exposed to low pH necessarily rub against the substrate in a particular way.
Mettam et al., 2012
Taken together, these studies support several possible explanations for the behavior, but they do not justify choosing a single cause without investigation.
Can a fish “scratch its gills”? The gill filaments lie inside the gill chamber, beneath the operculum (gill cover). When a fish makes external contact with a rock or the substrate, it may touch the skin of its head, the operculum, or the region of the gill opening. The gill filaments themselves do not necessarily make contact with the object.
It helps to distinguish three statements:
Observation: the fish makes a sudden rubbing movement against the substrate. Physiological hypothesis: gill irritation may have triggered this motor response. Assumption about the purpose of the movement: the fish is trying to scratch its gill filaments specifically. The second is entirely reasonable as a working hypothesis. The third is a much stronger claim: it assigns a specific purpose to the movement that cannot be inferred from the video alone.
Moreover, when a gill infestation is present, flashing may coexist with lesions on other external surfaces. Even confirmed gill monogeneans do not establish that every sideways contact with an aquarium decoration is directed specifically at the gills.
It is therefore more accurate to say “gill irritation may be accompanied by flashing” than to state categorically that “the fish is scratching its gills.”
Which observations are useful, and which are insufficient? A behavioral record can document the frequency of episodes, the side of the body involved, the area of contact, the sequence of movements, environmental conditions, and changes over time. All of these may be useful for subsequent analysis.
But the level of detail in an observation is not the same as its diagnostic specificity. Even a high-quality recording cannot, by itself, establish a parasitic cause if the relationship between a particular movement and that cause has not been validated.
In practical diagnosis, behavioral observations should be considered alongside other findings and examination results:
water parameters and recent changes in husbandry conditions; the condition of the skin, fins, and gill region, and the fish’s breathing pattern; how widespread the behavior is among fish in the system and how the signs change over time; when justified, microscopic examination of skin scrapings or appropriate gill samples, taking into account the risks of sampling for the fish. Such examinations help test competing explanations. For example, finding monogeneans is diagnostic evidence in its own right; it does not become evidence merely because the fish appeared to “scratch in a characteristic way.” Conversely, failing to see parasites in a superficial sample does not, by itself, exclude gill disease or other causes.
Observation, interpretation, diagnosis It is useful to distinguish three levels:
Level Example wording What remains unproven Observation “Repeated sudden lateral contacts with the substrate” Why they occur Interpretation “The behavior may be associated with skin or gill irritation” The source and location of the irritation Diagnostic hypothesis “Ectoparasitic infestation should be investigated” The presence and identity of a causative organism A hypothesis is not wrong simply because it has not yet been proven. The error occurs when it is recorded as an established fact.
We observe behavior. The cause of that behavior still needs to be demonstrated.
“You can tell by looking at the fish” may be the starting point of an informed professional suspicion. But for that suspicion to become a diagnostic criterion, we must be able to explain exactly what we are seeing and show how reliably it is associated with the proposed cause.

content:
Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. The fish is scratching A fish swims up to a rock, suddenly turns sideways, and brushes against it. A little later, it repeats the movement.
“The fish is scratching itself,” an observer might say.
Then perhaps: “There must be something wrong with its gills.” And after that: “It’s probably parasites.”
A familiar chain of reasoning. But these are three different claims — and the only thing we actually saw was the movement.
What did we actually see? We saw a fish rub against a surface. This behavior does occur in fish with certain diseases. In scientific studies, it is commonly called flashing or rubbing: a sudden sideways contact with an object or the bottom.
But the movement itself does not tell us why the fish did it.
Perhaps its skin is irritated. Perhaps the problem involves its gills. Perhaps something in the water is affecting it. Or perhaps the cause is something else entirely. The same action does not necessarily have the same cause.
“Scratching” is a convenient word in everyday conversation. But it already suggests an explanation we have not yet tested.
Two fish, one movement Imagine a test. In one aquarium, a fish has irritated skin because of unsuitable water conditions, such as excessively low pH. In another, a fish has parasitic worms — monogeneans — on its gills.
Now suppose both fish suddenly rub against the substrate. We are shown only video recordings, without being told what is happening in either aquarium.
Could we tell from the movement which fish is reacting to the water and which has parasites?
Perhaps their movements really do differ. But then we need to describe those differences: how the fish turns, which part of its body touches the surface, and how often the movement is repeated. Next, we would need to test whether those features actually help distinguish the causes.
If the only explanation is “you can just tell,” we have an impression, not evidence.
This is a thought experiment, not a description of a study that was actually performed. But it shows exactly what kind of evidence is missing.
Can a fish actually scratch its gills on a rock? Here is where things get interesting.
The gills are inside the gill chamber, protected by the gill cover (operculum). When a fish rubs against a rock, it touches the rock with the outside of its body — its skin, head, or gill cover.
Gill irritation really can be associated with this behavior. But that does not mean the fish is physically rubbing its gill filaments against the rock.
So there is a difference between these two statements:
“Gill irritation may cause this movement.”
And:
“The fish is scratching its gills.”
The first suggests a possible cause. The second sounds as though we already know exactly what the fish is trying to scratch. We do not.
What should you do if a fish starts rubbing against objects? Do not ignore the behavior. But do not diagnose a disease from a single movement either.
First, look for other changes: how the fish breathes and feeds, what its skin and fins look like, and whether other fish are behaving similarly. Check the water parameters. If there is reason to suspect parasites, examine an appropriate sample under the microscope.
Rubbing against objects is a useful signal to pay attention to the fish, not a ready-made explanation of the cause.
Studies have described this behavior in fish with parasitic infections (Garcia et al., 2014) and in fish with diseases involving marked skin changes (Maddocks et al., 2016). The sensitivity of fish nerve endings to chemical irritants, including low pH, has also been studied separately (Mettam et al., 2012). The latter study supports the possibility of chemical irritation, but does not demonstrate that low pH necessarily causes this particular rubbing behavior.
Where observation ends We can confidently say: “The fish suddenly brushes its side against the substrate.”
We can suggest: “Perhaps something is irritating it.”
But to say “It’s scratching its gills because of monogeneans” is to make several assumptions that still need to be tested.
We observe the behavior. Its cause still needs to be demonstrated.
Diagnosis begins with this distinction, not with guesswork.
Want to explore the subject further? F.O. — how to test an interpretation of fish behavior · F.O.S. — the full analysis with scientific references.
summary: We can see a fish rubbing against rocks. But can we see why? A story about the difference between observation and assumption.

Depth of analysis F. F.O. F.O.S. “Fin Rot”: A Diagnosis or a Description of Appearance? Irregular fin edges, shortened rays, whitish areas, and damaged fin membranes are often grouped under the familiar term “fin rot.” This is convenient in everyday conversation. In diagnosis, however, it creates a problem: the name itself already suggests an infectious cause, even though all we may have observed is tissue damage.
The same external change may result from trauma, a non-infectious pathological process, or a bacterial infection. These possibilities are not always mutually exclusive: microorganisms may colonize tissue that has already been damaged.
It is therefore useful to begin with three separate questions: what is damaged, how is the damage developing, and what caused it?
Fin damage is a morphological finding. Bacterial infection is one possible cause. The former does not automatically imply the latter.
What Is a Fin Ray Made Of? Structure of fin rays. A — segmented lepidotrichia. B — cross-section of a lepidotrichium showing its two half-segments. The supporting structures of bony fish fins are called lepidotrichia. They are segmented rays, not solid rods. Each lepidotrichium consists of two curved half-segments. Successive segments along the ray are connected by ligaments; connective tissue, blood vessels, and nerves lie between the half-segments. The entire structure is surrounded by the soft tissues of the fin (Sharples & Evans, 1996).
This combination of rigid elements and flexible connections gives the ray both strength and flexibility. But when the connections between its components are damaged, the segments may separate, split apart, or fragment. This does not necessarily mean that bacteria are directly destroying each of these elements.
What Does the Dissecting Needle Demonstrate? Ваш браузер не поддерживает видео. Separation of a damaged fin ray under a stereomicroscope In the video, the needle is applied to an already damaged fin ray. Its individual components separate along their connections, while some of the soft tissue remains intact in the area examined. Two conclusions need to be distinguished here.
Observation: the components of a damaged ray can separate under mechanical force. We can therefore observe a particular pattern of structural breakdown.
Cause not established: why the tissues and their connections were damaged before the needle was applied. Answering that requires information about the fish, its environment, and the nature of the lesion. The demonstration shows how the components separate when force is applied, but proves neither an infectious nor a non-infectious origin for the initial damage.
Fin Erosion Without a Primary Bacterial Infection The term fin erosion is used in scientific literature. It describes the breakdown of fin tissues, but the word “erosion” does not, by itself, establish an etiology: erosion may also occur in infectious diseases.
A particularly illustrative example is the study by Sharples and Evans (1996). The authors examined fin damage in goldfish (Carassius auratus) living in a section of river affected by pulp and paper mill effluent. Tissue examination allowed them to trace the sequence of pathological changes.
The outer epidermal structures were affected first: surface features were lost, and epithelial cells began to slough off. Changes in deeper tissues and the lepidotrichia appeared later. Substantial bacterial involvement was not found in most of the lesions examined; bacteria that were detected were considered likely secondary (Sharples & Evans, 1996).
What does this example demonstrate? A fin can deteriorate without an established primary bacterial infection. It does not prove that every similar lesion develops by the same mechanism or is necessarily associated with water pollution.
What If the Problem Is Nutrition or the Fish’s Overall Condition? Fin condition depends on more than the rigid rays. The integrity of the epithelium, connective tissue, and blood vessels, as well as tissue nutrition and the capacity for repair, are also important.
Dietary imbalances, disturbances in mineral metabolism, and the fish’s general physiological condition are reasonable areas to investigate. But it is easy to jump to another premature conclusion: seeing damaged fin tips and immediately attributing them to “poor tissue nutrition.”
Impaired tissue nutrition is a hypothesis that needs testing, not a label for every case of non-infectious erosion. In particular, general findings on mineral metabolism in fish do not demonstrate that the distal parts of fins must always be damaged first because of inadequate blood supply (Lall & Kaushik, 2021).
A lack of evidence for a bacterial cause is not evidence for any one particular non-infectious cause.
When Bacteria Contribute to Fin Destruction Bacteria found in infectious fin lesions. Left — filamentous forms; right — small rod-shaped bacteria. Bacterial diseases affecting fins do exist. In columnaris disease, associated with bacteria of the Flavobacterium columnare group, lesions of the skin, gills, and fins — including fin erosion — have been described (Declercq et al., 2013). In such cases, microorganisms may be direct participants in the pathological process.
But secondary bacterial processes also occur. Tissue is first damaged for another reason, and microorganisms subsequently colonize the altered surface. This is to be expected: fish are constantly exposed to diverse microbial communities, while their mucus and epithelium contribute to local defense (Gomez et al., 2013).
When interpreting a microscopic preparation, we need to consider not only whether bacteria are present, but also their distribution, their relationship to the damaged tissues, signs of inflammation, and the course of the disease. Finding large numbers of bacteria in a damaged area does not automatically tell us which event came first.
Two Different Scenarios Primary bacterial lesion: microorganisms contribute to the onset and progression of tissue damage.
Secondary colonization: the lesion develops first, and bacteria multiply on an already altered surface, potentially causing further complications.
Both scenarios are possible. In each case, the task is to determine which one best explains the observations.
A Practical Approach: Where to Start Instead of immediately prescribing a “fin rot treatment,” it is useful to assess several aspects in sequence:
Morphology. Which structures are damaged: the edges of the fin membrane, individual rays, or the fin base? Is there redness, a coating, mucus, necrosis, or hemorrhage? Progression. Did the damage develop rapidly or gradually? Is it still progressing? Distribution. Is one fish affected, a particular species, or many fish within the same system? Environment and injuries. Have there been changes in water conditions, filtration, equipment, transfers, aggression, or injuries during capture? Microscopy. What is happening to the soft tissues? Which microorganisms are present, and how are they associated with the affected area? If the findings suggest an infectious process, identifying the causative agent may require targeted sampling, bacterial culture, molecular testing, or histology. Yet even when these methods are unavailable, describing the tissues, performing microscopy, and examining husbandry conditions can narrow the range of possible explanations.
The limitations of the examination also matter: seeing bacteria does not establish their causal role, and failing to find bacteria in a single preparation does not completely rule out infection.
From Observation to Diagnosis We can document: “The edge of the caudal fin is irregular, individual rays are shortened, and the membrane between them is damaged.”
We can propose: “The lesion is consistent with fin erosion; traumatic, environmental, and infectious causes should be investigated.”
But stating “this is bacterial fin rot” requires independent supporting evidence, not merely a similar external appearance.
A diagnosis should explain the origin of the damage, not merely restate its appearance in different words.
First, describe the fin damage. Next, investigate the possible mechanisms. Only then decide what treatment is actually needed.
References Sharples, A. D., Evans, C. W. (1996). Pathology of fin erosion in goldfish Carassius auratus. Diseases of Aquatic Organisms, 24, 81–91. https://doi.org/10.3354/dao024081 Declercq, A. M. et al. (2013). Columnaris disease in fish: a review with emphasis on bacterium-host interactions. Veterinary Research, 44, 27. https://doi.org/10.1186/1297-9716-44-27 Gomez, D., Sunyer, J. O., Salinas, I. (2013). The mucosal immune system of fish: the evolution of tolerating commensals while fighting pathogens. Fish & Shellfish Immunology, 35, 1729–1739. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsi.2013.09.032 Lall, S. P., Kaushik, S. J. (2021). Nutrition and metabolism of minerals in fish. Animals, 11, 2711. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani11092711 Other levels: F. — a simple story about frayed fins · F.O.S. — full analysis and original research.
summary: From visible signs to underlying mechanisms: what the separation of lepidotrichia reveals, when bacteria cause fin damage, and how to investigate alternative explanations.
